records.themeTitle: Jacob’s own refinement does not finish the work of his descendants
records.themeSummary: Joseph’s turmoil shows Jacob that the clarification of his seed still requires awe and struggle, even when Jacob’s own heart is already refined.
records.targetEnglish: On his own part, Jacob had already attained the complete slaughter of the inclination, as it will be in the future, for the evil inclination is the angel of death, as stated in Bava Batra 16a. Through this he also merited that his bed was complete: none of his descendants would ultimately remain cast away. But among his descendants this is not yet clarified in this world; it awaits the future. He thought that he had already completed the repair, and sought to dwell in tranquility, seeing his world during his lifetime, something like the World to Come. Joseph’s turmoil then leaped upon him—that is, from the side of his descendants. As long as the inclination remains in the world, it is impossible to dwell in tranquility: one must always fear lest sin cause a loss, and must maintain restraints.
records.explanation: Divrei Soferim explains the distinction between the enduring promise that none of Jacob’s seed will be lost and the unfinished work of making that promise manifest. Jacob’s personal attainment therefore does not remove the need for care within the continuing life of his descendants. This develops the precise reason that Joseph’s turmoil interrupts the tranquility described here.
records.originHebrew: וְיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהָיָה לִבּוֹ מְבֹרָר שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לוֹ שׁוּם נְגִיעָה לְהַיֵּצֶר הָרָע, בִּקֵּשׁ לֵישֵׁב בְּשַׁלְוָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְהִתְעַנֵּג מֵהַקְּדֻשָּׁה, וְקָפַץ עָלָיו רָגְזוֹ שֶׁל יוֹסֵף, שֶׁהֶרְאוּ לוֹ מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם שֶׁעוֹד נִצְרָךְ בֵּרוּר בְּזַרְעוֹ, שֶׁכָּל זְמַן שֶׁהָאָדָם בַּחַיִּים יֵשׁ לוֹ עוֹד עֵסֶק שֶׁנִּצְרָךְ לְהִתְלַבֵּשׁ בְּיִרְאָה וּבְחִינַת הָרוֹגֶז שֶׁבַּקְּדֻשָּׁה.
records.originEnglish: And Jacob our Father, whose heart was completely refined without any contact with the Evil Inclination, sought to dwell in tranquil peace in this world delighting in holiness, and the agitation of Joseph bounded upon him, for Heaven showed him that further spiritual refining was required within his seed, since as long as man lives on earth he has ongoing labor requiring him to clothe himself in awe and holy agitation.
records.targetHebrew: דְּמִצִּדּוֹ כְּבָר זָכָה לִזְבִיחַת הַיֵּצֶר לְגַמְרֵי כִּלְעָתִיד, דְּהוּא יֵצֶר רָע הוּא מַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (ט״ז עַמּוּד א׳), וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה זָכָה גַּם כֵּן דְּמִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה, דְּגַם מִכָּל זַרְעוֹ לֹא יִדַּח נִדָּח, אֶלָּא שֶׁבְּזַרְעוֹ אֵינוֹ מְבֹרָר עֲדַיִן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה עַד לֶעָתִיד; וְהוּא שֶׁחָשַׁב שֶׁכְּבָר תִּקֵּן לְגַמְרֵי, בִּקֵּשׁ לֵישֵׁב בְּשַׁלְוָה לִרְאוֹת עוֹלָמוֹ בְּחַיָּיו מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא, וְקָפַץ רָגְזוֹ שֶׁל יוֹסֵף, הַיְינוּ מִצַּד זַרְעוֹ; וְכָל זְמַן שֶׁהַיֵּצֶר בָּעוֹלָם אִי אֶפְשָׁר לֵישֵׁב בְּשַׁלְוָה, וְצָרִיךְ לְיִרְאָה תָּמִיד שֶׁמָּא יִגְרֹם הַחֵטְא וּלְצִמְצוּמִים.

records.themeTitle: A holy root can appear through a faculty that also admits distortion
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok distinguishes the holy fear rooted in Isaac from the angry distortion associated with Esau, answering how the liver can belong to the divine pattern of the body.
records.targetEnglish: As the Talmud states in Chullin: whatever the Merciful One prohibited to us, He permitted its counterpart. He prohibited blood and permitted liver; menstrual blood, but the blood of purity; the forbidden fat of a domestic animal, but the fat of a wild animal; meat with milk, but the udder. Although the principal root of blood is the liver, as the Talmud states in Bekhorot, ‘The source of blood is the liver,’ and the principal root of meat with milk is the udder, nevertheless this is called the root, and at the place of the root there is no prohibition. This festival is called the giving of our Torah: a person recognizes that the essence and root of all creation is Torah. It would therefore be fitting that no prohibition stand before him. However, if a person does not recognize this clearly and takes these forbidden things into himself, they can bind him in cords and greatly disturb his mind. For the truth is that at the place of the root there is no prohibition, but in the branching out beyond the root there is prohibition. This is the meaning of ‘On Shavuot we also require something for you’: everyone agrees that this is the time when a person can receive all permitted things into himself, elevate them, and return them to the blessed God face to face.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef takes up the same apparently troubling example of liver and blood. It distinguishes a faculty’s root in Torah from the forms it takes as it branches into ordinary experience. This makes Rav Tzadok’s distinction between holy fear and distorted anger more intelligible. The excerpt retains Tiferet Yosef’s practical conclusion about receiving permitted things; its account of the root does not make the forbidden branches permissible.
records.originHebrew: וּלְהָבִין הָעִנְיָן: הֲלֹא כָּל הָאֵיבָרִים הֵמָּה כְּדֻגְמָא דִּלְעֵילָא, כְּמַה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם בְּצַלְמֵנוּ וְגוֹמֵר", וְאֵיךְ שַׁיָּךְ הַכָּבֵד שֶׁהוּא עֵשָׂו, מִדַּת הַכַּעַס, בְּשֹׁרֶשׁ הַקְּדֻשָּׁה? אָמְנָם יֵשׁ לוֹמַר שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת יֵשׁ שְׁנֵי עִנְיָנִים בְּרֹגֶז: עִנְיַן הָרוֹגֶז שֶׁל כַּעַס הוּא דַּרְגָּא דְּעֵשָׂו, שֶׁהוּא הַפְּסֹלֶת דִּגְבוּרָה דְּיִצְחָק שֶׁבַּקְּדֻשָּׁה; וְיֵשׁ רוֹגֶז בִּקְדֻשָּׁה שֶׁנִּקְרָא "פַּחַד יִצְחָק", וְהַיְנוּ הַיִּרְאָה וְהַפַּחַד מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְבַל יַעֲבֹר רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ.
records.originEnglish: and to understand the matter: are not all bodily organs patterned after the heavenly realm above, as stated: "Let us make man in our image, etc.", so how does the liver, representing Esau and fury, exist in the root of holiness? However, one can explain that in truth there are two dimensions within rogez (agitation): the agitation of angry fury is the level of Esau, which is the waste product of Isaac's holy Gevurah; and there is holy agitation called the "Fear of Isaac", meaning awe and dread before the Blessed Name lest one transgress His Blessed Will.
records.targetHebrew: וכדאיתא בש"ס (חולין קט:) כל מה דאסר לן רחמנא שרא לן כותיה אסר לן דמא שרא לן כבדא נדה דם טוהר חלב בהמה חלב חיה בשר בחלב כחל. ואף שבאמת עיקר שורש של הדם הוא הכבד, וכדאיתא בש"ס (בכורות נה:) זכרותא דדמא כבדא, והעיקר השורש של בשר בחלב הוא כחל, מ"מ יען שזה נקרא השורש, ובמקום השורש אין שום איסור. וזה החג שנקרא מתן תורתינו, והיינו שהאדם מכיר זאת שעיקר והשורש של כל הבריאה הוא ד"ת, אז היה מן הראוי שלא יהיה שום איסור נגדו. אך מחמת שאם האדם אינו מכיר זאת מפורש ויקבל לתוכו את אלו הדברים האסורים, יוכלו לאסרהו בעבותות ויטרידו את דעתו ביותר, כי האמת הוא שבמקום השורש אין שום איסור, אך בהסתעפות להלן מן השורש שם הוא איסור. וזה הענין בעצרת דבעינן נמי לכם, שזה כולי עלמא מודים שאז הוא הזמן שיכול לקבל כל דברים המותרים לתוכו, ויכול להעלות אותם ולהחזירם להשי"ת פנים בפנים:

records.themeTitle: The heart’s competing impulses need the guidance of Oral Torah
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok identifies the heart’s pure life with awe that prevents a person from defying God’s will; learning without that heart is deficient.
records.targetEnglish: The foundation of Oral Torah is the completion of deeds: the practical law of how to conduct oneself in all one’s ways and paths in matters of action. The aspect of blood is the nefesh, which is ‘at the head of all illnesses,’ as stated in Bava Batra 58b. As explained above in chapter three, the heart is balanced, half meritorious and half liable: tendencies toward both good and evil are implanted in it by nature. The Sages call these the good inclination and the evil inclination. As stated in Berakhot 61b, ‘A wise person’s heart is to his right,’ in the right chamber of the heart, and ‘a fool’s heart is to his left.’ The aspect of the neshamah belongs wholly to God, as the Men of the Great Assembly instituted that we say, ‘My God, the soul You placed within me is pure.’ The aspect of the nefesh is the reverse: it is mixed and kneaded together with the material body, and therefore tends especially after it. It is ‘at the head of all illnesses.’ ‘At the head of all remedies am I, wine’: wine is Oral Torah, the liquid that emerges from the vine. Our Sages said, ‘The vine—these are Israel.’ Elsewhere I explained the teaching that words of Torah are compared to these three liquids, water, wine, and milk. Wine specifically alludes to Oral Torah: it resembles the wine in that it flows from the hearts of Israel’s sages and emerges from their minds and understanding. This is foremost among the remedies for all the illnesses that emerge from bad blood, because it guides every part of action to be conducted in accordance with God’s will.
records.explanation: Sichat Malakhei HaSharet explains why the heart needs guidance: it contains impulses in both directions, while Oral Torah works out how conduct can follow God’s will. Its account of Torah as a remedy gives practical content to the pure blood and awe described here. The comparison concerns Rav Tzadok’s account of the soul and conduct, with the physiological imagery kept in its original conceptual setting.
records.originHebrew: אָמְנָם יֵשׁ בּוֹ רְבִיעִית דָּם שֶׁהוּא צַחוּתָא דְּדָמָא הַנִּתָּן לַלֵּב (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרַעְיָא מְהֵימְנָא שָׁם וְתוֹסָפוֹת סוֹטָה ה׳ עַמּוּד א׳), וְהַיְנוּ בְּחִינַת הָרוֹגֶז שֶׁבַּקְּדֻשָּׁה, וְהוּא הַיִּרְאָה הַנִּצְרָךְ לַלֵּב; וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (יוֹמָא ע״ב עַמּוּד ב׳) שֶׁעַל הָעוֹסְקִין בַּתּוֹרָה וְאֵין בָּהֶם יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם נֶאֱמַר: "לָמָּה זֶּה מְחִיר בְּיַד כְּסִיל לִקְנוֹת חָכְמָה וְלֵב אָיִן", כִּי זֶהוּ עֶצֶם שֹׁרֶשׁ הַלֵּב: לִהְיוֹת מָלֵא יִרְאָה וּפַחַד מִלַּמְרוֹת עֵינֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
records.originEnglish: however, there resides within it a revi'it of blood which is the radiant clarity of blood given to the heart (as written in Ra'aya Meheimna ibid. and Tosafot Sotah 5a), meaning the aspect of holy trembling, which is the awe essential to the heart; as written (Yoma 72b) that regarding those studying Torah without fear of Heaven it is said: "Why is there a price in the hand of a fool to acquire wisdom, seeing he has no heart", for this is the very foundation of the heart: to be brimming with awe and dread against rebelling before the eyes of the Blessed Name.
records.targetHebrew: כִּי יְסוֹד תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הוּא הַשְׁלָמַת הַמַּעֲשִׂים, שֶׁהוּא הַדְּבַר הֲלָכָה, כֵּיצַד לְהִתְנַהֵג בְּכָל הֲלִיכוֹתָיו וּדְרָכָיו בְּעִנְיְנֵי הַמַּעֲשִׂים. וְחֵלֶק הַדָּם הוּא הַנֶּפֶשׁ שֶׁהוּא בְּרֵישׁ כָּל מַרְעִין כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא נ״ח עַמּוּד ב׳); וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר לְעֵיל (פֶּרֶק ג׳), כִּי הַלֵּב הוּא שָׁקוּל מֶחֱצָה זַכַּאי וּמֶחֱצָה חַיָּב, רָצָה לוֹמַר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ נְטִיָּה לְטוֹב וּנְטִיָּה לְרַע מֻטְבָּעִים בּוֹ, וְהֵם הַנִּקְרָאִים בְּפִי הַחֲכָמִים: יֵצֶר טוֹב וְיֵצֶר הָרָע, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא (בְּרָכוֹת ס״א עַמּוּד ב׳): כִּי "לֵב חָכָם לִימִינוֹ" [קֹהֶלֶת י׳:ב׳] — בֶּחָלָל יָמִין שֶׁבַּלֵּב, וְ"לֵב כְּסִיל לִשְׂמֹאלוֹ" [שָׁם]. וְחֵלֶק הַנְּשָׁמָה הוּא כֻּלּוֹ לַה', כְּמוֹ שֶׁתִּקְּנוּ אַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה לוֹמַר: "אֱלֹהַי, נְשָׁמָה שֶׁנָּתַתָּ בִּי טְהוֹרָה [הִיא]". וְחֵלֶק הַנֶּפֶשׁ הוּא לְהֵיפֶךְ, כִּי הוּא הַמְמֻסָּךְ וּמְגֻבָּל עִם הַגּוּף הַחָמְרִי, וּלְכָךְ נְטִיָּתוֹ אַחֲרָיו בְּיִחוּד, וְהוּא "בְּרֵישׁ כָּל מַרְעִין". וּ"בְרֵישׁ כָּל אַסְוָון — אֲנָא חֲמַר" [בָּבָא בַּתְרָא שָׁם]: הַיַּיִן הוּא תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שֶׁהוּא הַמַּשְׁקִין הַיּוֹצֵא מִן הַגֶּפֶן, וּכְבָר אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (חֻלִּין צ״ב [עַמּוּד א׳]): "גֶּפֶן" — אֵלּוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל; וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר עַל מַה שֶּׁאִיתָא (תַּעֲנִית ז׳ עַמּוּד א׳) שֶׁנִּמְשְׁלוּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה לִג׳ מַשְׁקִין הַלָּלוּ: מַיִם, וְיַיִן, וְחָלָב, שֶׁהַיַּיִן בְּיִחוּד רוֹמֵז לְבַד עַל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שֶׁהוּא דֻּגְמָתוֹ, שֶׁהוּא הַנּוֹבֵעַ מִלֵּב חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְהַיּוֹצֵא מִתּוֹךְ מֹחָם וְדַעְתָּם. וְזֶהוּ בְּרֵאשׁ הָרְפוּאוֹת לְכָל הַחֳלָיִים הַיּוֹצְאִין מִדָּם הָרָע, כִּי הוּא הַמַּדְרִיךְ לְחֶלְקֵי הַמַּעֲשִׂים כֻּלָּם שֶׁיִּהְיוּ מוּנְהָגִים כְּפִי רְצוֹן ה'.

records.themeTitle: Looking at creation can become a question about its Creator
records.themeSummary: Guarding the eyes culminates in directing sight toward ‘Who created these,’ giving the faculty of seeing a positive purpose.
records.targetEnglish: The meaning is that when Abraham saw the opposing powers described above give way before one another, he understood that the blessed God had not concealed Himself completely. God therefore established two opposites, so that through both people would recognize that there is One higher than them who rules them, and would look only toward Him. For this reason God also established male and female in every matter in the world. Likewise it is written, ‘Lift your eyes on high and see: Who created these?’ ‘These’ means all the particulars that God established in the world. ‘Who’ is the place open to questioning: a person should seek to know Who created these. For this purpose God created all the particulars called ‘these,’ as stated in the introduction to the holy Zohar, 1b, and as explained in the portion of Bereshit. God desires that created beings ask Who the Creator is; He therefore created opposing things in the world.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov explains the movement within the verse that Rav Tzadok uses to redirect the eyes. Visible particulars and opposing powers prompt a question about their common source. Guarding sight can therefore develop into attentive inquiry that leads beyond the visible object to the One who gives it existence. The preceding paragraph identifies Abraham’s observations of sun and moon, supplying the opening antecedent.
records.targetRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 3:10

records.themeTitle: Dan’s union with Judah includes the transforming power of repentance
records.themeSummary: The lowest tribe joins the highest in the building of the sanctuary. Rav Tzadok reads this union as a foretaste of the future joining of the end to the beginning.
records.targetEnglish: But in truth the handmaids too gave birth to the tribes of God. Nevertheless, the first child born to Rachel’s handmaid was Dan, the lowest of the tribes, ‘the rear guard of all the camps,’ who traveled last. Our Sages said that the cloud expelled some of them, for they were outside Israel’s camp: in them was the root of anger, as it says in Judges 18:25 that they were bitter of spirit. They also said in Bekhorot 55a that the Jordan descends from Dan; the Jordan alludes to anger, as explained above. Likewise, ‘Dan shall be a serpent upon the road.’ Therefore she said, ‘God has judged me’: He stirred the attribute of judgment and anger, and this child was born through that attribute, by His blessed agency. Its use was permitted through this holy attribute of His, for in truth this power is holy in Dan. Therefore he is always joined to Judah. David too was ruddy, but ‘with beautiful eyes’: he killed only with the Sanhedrin’s judgment. Only through the power of repentance does evil become very good, until Dan ‘judges his people as one’—like the distinguished one among the tribes.
records.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim supplies an inner mechanism for the joining of Dan and Judah: anger is directed through holy judgment, and Judah’s repentance transforms a defect into good. This develops what the architectural partnership signifies in Rav Tzadok’s paragraph. The source explains repentance and judgment; the image of the circle remains the distinctive further step made here in Pri Tzadik.
records.targetRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:13

records.themeTitle: The future circle discloses everyone’s dependence on God
records.themeSummary: In the future circle, the end joins the beginning. This makes the meeting of Dan and Judah an image of hope for one at the lowest point.
records.targetEnglish: If he overcomes it, well and good; if not, he should recite the Shema. For there can be self-exaltation within words of Torah, and through words of Torah a person can embolden himself, so that he cannot reach true clarification. The counsel for this is to recite the Shema. The meaning of the Shema is like the Talmud’s teaching in Ta’anit 31a: in the future the Holy One will make a circle for the righteous. That is, everyone will see that everything is in God’s hands, and no one has any advantage or exalted standing over his fellow. A circle is something round that has no end. This is what the Shema alludes to.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explains the circle through the recognition that every person depends upon God. This illuminates why Rav Tzadok can use that image to join the lowest tribe to the highest: their relation is seen from the common divine source. Mei HaShiloach also brings that future recognition into present service through the Shema and the removal of spiritual self-exaltation.
records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayigash 4

records.themeTitle: Jacob’s hidden root becomes a felt awareness within Israel’s hearts
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok moves from faith that God stands over a person to the illumination of truth that becomes perceptible in the heart; he associates this renewal with Jacob.
records.targetEnglish: The King of the world is the human form upon the throne, which is the likeness of Jacob our father, peace be upon him, as stated in Chullin 91b and Bereshit Rabbah 68. This means the hidden root of all the souls of Israel in every generation, whose root is included in Jacob our father: the children are hidden potentially within the father. The individual souls that constitute the congregation of Israel are His Shekhinah—that is, God’s dwelling within Israel’s hearts in the revealed awareness of the heart. The root in the depths of the heart, through which all Israel cleave to God, including Israel’s sinners—for even though one has sinned, one remains Israel, because ‘the Lord’s portion is His people, Jacob’—is the human form of the divine chariot. Although it is always Jacob’s likeness, it is not identical in every generation; it corresponds to the souls of that generation. Every generation unfolds the stature of Jacob, yet they are not precisely the same, just as a person’s appearance sometimes changes, from red to white and the like. The familiar unification of the Holy One and His Shekhinah occurs when the holiness of the hidden root in the depths of the heart is drawn into the heart’s revealed awareness, so that one feels His divinity in the heart, as though standing before the King. This is stated in the gloss at the beginning of Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim, on the verse ‘I have set the Lord before me.’
records.explanation: Divrei Soferim unfolds the relation between Jacob and the congregation of Israel that is compressed into the sun and moon imagery here. Jacob represents the hidden common root; the individual hearts receive its disclosed holiness. This explains the paragraph’s transition from a truth held through faith to a truth felt in the heart, while preserving the shared reference to standing before the King.

records.originEnglish: and Jewish souls as Knesset Yisrael possess the capacity to accept the yoke of Heaven in the heart through faith, as written at the very opening of the Rama's gloss on the Shulchan Aruch: "'I have set Hashem always before me, etc.', when a person reflects that the King, the Holy One, stands over him, etc., immediately there will arrive to him fear, submission, and dread of the Blessed Name." And this is the foundation of the entire Shulchan Aruch: that man must fix this in his heart that the King of kings stands over him, which operates purely through faith in the heart, even if he does not perceive it tangibly. However, when one receives light from the sun, as stated: "For a sun and a shield is Hashem", meaning when there shines within his heart a revelation of Godliness in the realm of Truth, this is the essence of the renewal of the moon, and this is the Rosh Chodesh wherein the aspect of Jacob shines upon Knesset Yisrael, which is the point of Truth, as stated: "You give truth to Jacob";

records.themeTitle: Faith can sustain awareness of providence beyond what one presently grasps
records.themeSummary: The first acceptance of God’s kingship rests on faith, even before a person perceives the divine presence tangibly.
records.targetEnglish: The principal protection for a person then is to establish firmly in his heart an abundant faith in His providence. This is like the holy Zohar’s explanation in Vayera 103b of ‘Her husband is known at the gates’: this is the Holy One, who becomes known and apprehended according to what each person estimates within his heart, as far as he can cleave with the spirit of wisdom. According to what he estimates in his heart, so is He known in his heart; hence ‘known at the gates,’ through those gates. This means that His providence over a person corresponds, for each one, to what he holds within his heart. If a person establishes abundant faith that God always watches over him, even beyond what his understanding grasps, God indeed conducts Himself with that person accordingly, guarding him even at that moment of transition that appears empty. From the perspective of a person who so believes in His providence, there is no essential difference between the middle of a season and the transition between seasons. Even in the middle of a season, which lies within his understanding, he follows with great faith God’s providence, which lies beyond what his understanding grasps.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim describes how faith functions when a person reaches the limits of present comprehension. Awareness of providence cultivated in ordinary conditions can continue through an interval whose meaning is not yet perceptible. This develops the initial faith described here before the subsequent illumination of truth. Its setting is a transition between seasons; it is not a separate identification of Jacob with the new moon.
records.targetRef: Sod Yesharim, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot 21:1

records.themeTitle: Clearing desire and receiving light strengthen one another
records.themeSummary: Joseph’s guarded covenant prepares the heart for Jacob’s truth: a heart filled with desires cannot receive that illumination.
records.targetEnglish: To the extent that a person distances himself from evil—that is, from all the attractions of this world and desires directed toward himself—he draws close to God and attains His light, as it says, ‘Bring us back, and cause Your face to shine.’ Conversely, to the extent that he attains awareness of God, he distances himself from worldly matters, as expressed by ‘I am’ and ‘You shall have no other.’ Of this they said, ‘If there is no awe, there is no wisdom; if there is no wisdom, there is no awe.’ Wisdom is apprehension of God, and awe is fear of sin; neither suffices without the other. Awe is called a storehouse and a vessel of reception: the heart empties itself of all kinds of desires and attractions and thereby becomes an empty vessel to receive words of Torah. As our Sages say: when a word of mockery leaves, a word of Torah enters; when a word of Torah leaves, a word of mockery enters. When the heart is empty of Torah, it is ready to receive every kind of desire, for it cannot remain wholly empty. Therefore the two go together. Neither precedes the other beyond an instant; the other level follows immediately. When a person turns his heart toward God, God immediately causes His light to rest there. Awe is what God asks of people, as it says, ‘What does the Lord your God ask of you, but to fear’; wisdom is what God bestows, as it says, ‘He gives wisdom to the wise,’ and, ‘For the Lord gives wisdom.’ The awakening from below must come first. Of this they said, ‘Open for Me like the point of a needle’: even the smallest awe suffices, and a corresponding measure of wisdom will then flow into the heart. Through the wisdom more awe comes, then more wisdom, and so on, until there are openings large enough for wagons and carriages to enter, as the cited Midrash continues. The early teachers said: provided that the opening passes through from side to side. This means a complete awakening from the depths of the heart to abandon sin and relinquish all worldly concerns; even a single moment is enough.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik explains the relationship as a continuing exchange. A sincere clearing of the heart makes room for illumination; that illumination deepens the capacity for awe and further clearing. This supplies the inner process by which Joseph’s guarding makes Jacob’s truth receivable, and shows why even a small but wholehearted beginning can matter.
records.originHebrew: וְעִם כָּל זֶה נִצְרָךְ לָזֶה גַּם קְדֻשַּׁת יוֹסֵף: לִהְיוֹת נִשְׁמָר בְּרוּחוֹ לְהַחֲזִיק בִּמְעֻזּוֹ בְּיִרְאַת הַשֵּׁם לִהְיוֹת שׁוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה נַעֲשָׂה הַהִתְקַשְּׁרוּת וְיִחוּד קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא וּשְׁכִינְתֵיהּ, דְּהַיְנוּ יִחוּד אֱמֶת וֶאֱמוּנָה עַל יְדֵי בְּחִינַת יוֹסֵף; כִּי אִי אֶפְשָׁר לִכְנוֹס בַּלֵּב הֶאָרַת הָאֱמֶת וְלִהְיוֹת "הַשֵּׁם אוֹרִי" כְּשֶׁהַלֵּב מָלֵא תַּאֲווֹת. וְעַל יְדֵי קְדֻשַּׁת יוֹסֵף יְכוֹלִים לִזְכּוֹת לִקְדֻשַּׁת יַעֲקֹב, בְּחִינַת אֱמֶת.
records.originEnglish: And nonetheless there is required for this also the holiness of Joseph: to be guarded in his spirit holding fast to his stronghold in the fear of Hashem, guarding the Covenant, whereby is achieved the connection and unification of the Holy One and His Shechinah, which is the union of Truth and Faith through the agency of Joseph; for it is impossible for the light of Truth to enter the heart and experience "Hashem is my light" when the heart is brimming with physical lusts. And through the holiness of Joseph one can merit the holiness of Jacob, the dimension of Truth.
records.targetHebrew: כְּפִי הִתְרַחֲקוּת הָאָדָם מִן הָרַע, וְהַיְינוּ מִכָּל חֲמוּדוֹת הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וּתְשׁוּקוֹת דִּלְגַרְמֵיהּ, כָּךְ הוּא מִתְקָרֵב לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וּמַשִּׂיג אוֹרוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ... וְהָאֵר פָּנֶיךָ" (תְּהִלִּים פ, ד). וְכֵן לְהֵיפֶךְ: כְּפִי הַשָּׂגָתוֹ מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כָּךְ מִתְרַחֵק מֵעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אָנֹכִי" וְ"לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ". וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ: אִם אֵין יִרְאָה אֵין חָכְמָה, אִם אֵין חָכְמָה אֵין יִרְאָה (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ג, יז). חָכְמָה הוּא הַשָּׂגַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְיִרְאָה הוּא מִן הַחֵטְא, וְהָא בְּלָא הָא לָא סַגִּי. וְיִרְאָה נִקְרָא "אוֹצָר" וּכְלִי קִבּוּל, שֶׁהַלֵּב מִתְפַּנֶּה מִכָּל מִינֵי תְּשׁוּקוֹת וַחֲמוּדוֹת, וּמִמֵּילָא הוּא כְּלִי פָּנוּי לְקַבֵּל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: יָצָא דָּבָר שֶׁל לֵיצָנוּת – נִכְנַס דָּבָר שֶׁל תּוֹרָה, יָצָא דָּבָר שֶׁל תּוֹרָה – נִכְנַס שֶׁל לֵיצָנוּת. כִּי כְּשֶׁהַלֵּב פָּנוּי מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, מִמֵּילָא הוּא מוּכָן לְקַבֵּל כָּל מִינֵי תַּאֲווֹת, כִּי אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה פָּנוּי לְגַמְרֵי. וּלְכָךְ הֵם שְׁנֵיהֶם בְּיַחַד וְאֵין הָאֶחָד קוֹדֵם לַחֲבֵירוֹ רַק בְּרֶגַע כְּמֵימְרֵיהּ, אֲבָל תֵּיכֶף תָּכוּף לוֹ מַדְרֵגָה הָאַחֶרֶת. וְהַמְפַנֶּה לִבּוֹ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, תֵּיכֶף הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁרֶה אוֹרוֹ שָׁם; כִּי הַיִּרְאָה הִיא מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שׁוֹאֵל מִבְּנֵי אָדָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְעַתָּה... מָה ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ שֹׁאֵל מֵעִמָּךְ כִּי אִם לְיִרְאָה]" (דְּבָרִים י, יב), וְהַחָכְמָה מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁפִּיעַ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "יָהֵב חָכְמְתָא לְחַכִּימִין]" (דָּנִיֵּאל ב, כא), וְנֶאֱמַר: "כִּי ה' יִתֵּן חָכְמָה וְגוֹמֵר" (מִשְׁלֵי ב, ו). וְאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת מִקּוֹדֶם, וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה ה, ב): "פִּתְחוּ לִי כְּחֻדָּהּ שֶׁל מַחַט", כִּי דַּי בְּכָל שֶׁהוּא יִרְאָה, וְאָז יֻשְׁפַּע בְּלִבּוֹ נֶגְדּוֹ כָּךְ חָכְמָה. וּמִמֵּילָא עַל יְדֵי הַחָכְמָה תָּבִיא לוֹ עוֹד יִרְאָה, וְאָז תָּבוֹא עוֹד חָכְמָה, וְחוֹזֵר חָלִילָה עַד שֶׁיִּהְיוּ פְּתָחִים שֶׁיִּהְיוּ וְכוּלֵי. וְאָמְרוּ קַדְמוֹנִים: וּבִלְבַד שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נֶקֶב מְפוּלָּשׁ מֵעֵבֶר לְעֵבֶר, וּרְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מִמַּעֲמַקֵּי לִבּוֹ הִתְעוֹרְרוּת גָּמוּר דַּעֲזִיבַת הַחֵטְא, וְלַעֲזוֹב כָּל עִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, אֲפִילּוּ רֶגַע אֶחָד דַּי:

records.themeTitle: Turning desire toward God prepares a clearer revelation
records.themeSummary: The heart must be freed from competing desires in order to receive the illumination of truth.
records.targetEnglish: It is written in Malachi 3:20, ‘For you who fear My name, a sun of righteousness will shine, with healing in its wings.’ ‘Those who fear My name’ means those who have a grasp of words of Torah and of God, which obligates them in true awe. That is the meaning of ‘those who fear My name.’ God promises them that a sun of righteousness will shine for them: clear words of Torah. ‘Healing in its wings’ means security and strength in God and in words of Torah, like wings, which are a strong protection for winged creatures. Before God was revealed to Abraham our father, he found no rest in all the matters of this world and rejected them. His principal longing was to know Who was the master of the palace. As it says in Proverbs 15:24, ‘The path of life is upward for the discerning’: this was the chief and foremost thing for him, like something placed above. Therefore God appeared to him and gave him strength in clear words of Torah. Elonei denotes strength; Mamre indicates that he resisted and rebelled against all worldly matters. ‘He was sitting at the entrance of the tent in the heat of the day’: love of God, who is called ‘day,’ grew warm and ardent within him and was clear before him. This is the meaning of ‘the entrance of the tent’: it was open before him.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach shows the positive direction of the heart’s clearing. Abraham’s dissatisfaction with worldly matters becomes a longing to know their Master, and that longing is answered with clearer Torah and a sense of divine security. This helps explain why the guarded heart in Pri Tzadik is a preparation for illumination: its desire has acquired a different object and purpose.
records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayera 1
records.originHebrew: וְעִם כָּל זֶה נִצְרָךְ לָזֶה גַּם קְדֻשַּׁת יוֹסֵף: לִהְיוֹת נִשְׁמָר בְּרוּחוֹ לְהַחֲזִיק בִּמְעֻזּוֹ בְּיִרְאַת הַשֵּׁם לִהְיוֹת שׁוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה נַעֲשָׂה הַהִתְקַשְּׁרוּת וְיִחוּד קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא וּשְׁכִינְתֵיהּ, דְּהַיְנוּ יִחוּד אֱמֶת וֶאֱמוּנָה עַל יְדֵי בְּחִינַת יוֹסֵף; כִּי אִי אֶפְשָׁר לִכְנוֹס בַּלֵּב הֶאָרַת הָאֱמֶת וְלִהְיוֹת "הַשֵּׁם אוֹרִי" כְּשֶׁהַלֵּב מָלֵא תַּאֲווֹת. וְעַל יְדֵי קְדֻשַּׁת יוֹסֵף יְכוֹלִים לִזְכּוֹת לִקְדֻשַּׁת יַעֲקֹב, בְּחִינַת אֱמֶת.

records.targetHebrew: כְּתִיב (מַלְאָכִי גִּימֶל, כָּף) "וְזָרְחָה לָכֶם יִרְאֵי שְׁמִי שֶׁמֶשׁ צְדָקָה וּמַרְפֵּא בִּכְנָפֶיהָ". "יִרְאֵי שְׁמִי", הַיְינוּ מִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ תְּפִיסָה בְּדִבְרֵי תּוֹרָה וּבְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְזֹאת יְחַיֵּיב לָהֶם הַיִּרְאָה הָאֲמִיתִּיּוֹת, וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ "יִרְאֵי שְׁמִי" וּמַבְטִיחַ לָהֶם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כִּי יָאִיר לָהֶם שֶׁמֶשׁ צְדָקָה הַיְינוּ דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה מְבוֹרָרִין. "וּמַרְפֵּא בִּכְנָפֶיהָ", הַיְינוּ בְּטוּחוֹת וְעֹז בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וּבְדִבְרֵי תּוֹרָה כְּמוֹ הַכְּנָפַיִם שֶׁהֵם מִבְטַח עֹז לְבַעֲלֵי הַכָּנָף. וְהִנֵּה אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם קֹדֶם שֶׁנִּגְלָה אֵלָיו הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לֹא הָיָה לוֹ שׁוּם נַיְיחָא מִכָּל עִנְיְינֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְהָיָה מְמָאֵס בָּהֶם וְעִיקָּר הָיָה אֶצְלוֹ תְּשׁוּקָה לֵידַע מִי הוּא בַּעַל הַבִּירָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (מִשְׁלֵי טֵית וָאו, כָּף דָּלֶת) "אֹרַח חַיִּים לְמַעְלָה לְמַשְׂכִּיל", הַיְינוּ כִּי זֹאת הָיָה אֶצְלוֹ עִיקָּר וָרֹאשׁ לְכָל דָּבָר כְּמוֹ דָּבָר שֶׁמּוּנָּח לְמַעְלָה, עַל כֵּן נִרְאָה אֵלָיו הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְנָתַן לוֹ תַּקּוּפוּת, לְדִבְרֵי תּוֹרָה מְבוֹרָרִים. כִּי אֵלוֹנֵי הוּא לְשׁוֹן תַּקּוּפוּת וּמַמְרֵא הַיְינוּ לְפִי שֶׁסֵּירֵב וּמָרָה בְּכָל עִנְיְינֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה. "וְהוּא יֹשֵׁב פֶּתַח הָאֹהֶל כְּחֹם הַיּוֹם", הַיְינוּ שֶׁהָיָה מִתְחַמֵּם וּמִתְלַהֵב בּוֹ אַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁנִּקְרָא יוֹם, וְהָיָה מְפוֹרָשׁ לְפָנָיו. וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ "פֶּתַח הָאֹהֶל" הַיְינוּ שֶׁהָיָה פָּתוּחַ לְפָנָיו.

records.themeTitle: The moral direction of strength distinguishes holy restraint from anger
records.themeSummary: The trembling that restrains a person before God differs from Esau’s jealousy and anger, even though both are associated with strength.
records.targetEnglish: ‘God made this corresponding to that.’ That is, God gave a person the choice either to benefit another through his kindness and administer justice against the wicked, or to benefit himself through evil desires—as the Baal Shem Tov explained the verse ‘A person’s desire is his kindness’—and to benefit God’s enemies. As in the familiar saying, “Every adulterer is good to other people”; ‘You shall not murder’ and ‘You shall not commit adultery’ are two opposites, as I wrote elsewhere. One can also harm those who love God through an evil form of strength, from which come jealousy, anger, and murder.
records.explanation: Kometz explains why the name of a faculty does not establish its moral character. Kindness and strength take their character from whom and what they serve. This clarifies the distinction in Pri Tzadik: holy strength checks the inclination under God’s authority, while distorted strength turns against what should be protected. The account of choice also explains why an outward resemblance between two reactions is insufficient to identify them.
records.originHebrew: אַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת לְשׁוֹן "רוֹגֶז" נִמְצָא בַּמִּקְרָא עַל הָרֹב עַל הַחֲרָדָה וּרְעָדָה, וְהוּא "פַּחַד יִצְחָק", שֶׁעוֹמֵד פַּחַד הַשֵּׁם לְנֶגֶד עֵינָיו, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (שָׁם ה׳ עַמּוּד א׳): "לְעוֹלָם יַרְגִּיז אָדָם יֵצֶר טוֹב עַל יֵצֶר הָרָע, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: 'רִגְזוּ וְאַל תֶּחֱטָאוּ'", שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַחֲרָדָה שֶׁיַּכְנִיס בְּלִבּוֹ מִפַּחַד הַשֵּׁם עַל יְדֵי זֶה יְנַצַּח הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע. וּמִיִּצְחָק יָצָא הַפְּסֹלֶת עֵשָׂו שֶׁהוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ הַקִּנְאָה וְהַכַּעַס, וּכְתִיב: "כַּעַס בְּחֵיק כְּסִילִים יָנוּחַ", וּ"כְסִיל" נִקְרָא מִי שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנִּדְרַשׁ (יוֹמָא ע״ב עַמּוּד ב׳) "לָמָּה זֶּה מְחִיר בְּיַד כְּסִיל" עַל הָעוֹסְקִין בַּתּוֹרָה וְאֵין בָּהֶם יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם;
records.originEnglish: However, in truth the term rogez is found in Scripture mostly denoting trembling and dread, and this is the "Fear of Isaac", where the fear of Hashem stands before his eyes, and as written (ibid. 5a): "A person should always agitate the Good Inclination against the Evil, as it is said: 'Tremble and sin not'", for through the trembling he introduces into his heart from fear of God, he conquers the Evil Inclination. And from Isaac issued the refuse, Esau, who is the root of envy and fury, and it is written: "Anger rests in the bosom of fools", and a "fool" is anyone devoid of fear of Heaven, as expounded (Yoma 72b) regarding "Why is there a price in the hand of a fool" on those studying Torah without fear of Heaven;

records.themeTitle: A forceful response is needed only while it checks an evil desire
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok describes holy trembling as a means of overcoming the evil inclination.
records.targetEnglish: ‘He sent out the raven, and it went back and forth.’ The raven alludes to anger. Noah wanted the attribute of anger to be absent from the world, but the Holy One showed him that, for the time being, this attribute is still needed in the world. Sometimes, when an evil desire comes to a person, he can save himself by arousing anger within himself. This is the meaning of ‘It went back and forth until the water dried’: until evil desires disappear from the world, then anger too will cease, for water signifies desire. Therefore a small indication of this began in the Temple, where there was an amah called ‘the raven deterrent,’ as stated in Middot 4:6.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explains the limited purpose and duration of this forceful response. It serves to interrupt a harmful desire, and loses its purpose when such desires disappear. This develops Rav Tzadok’s use of agitation against the inclination as an instrument of restraint. It also prepares for the later Chanukah discussion of a future state in which this struggle is no longer needed.

records.themeTitle: True wisdom deepens humility by revealing where wisdom comes from
records.themeSummary: The bent ayin represents submission before God. Rav Tzadok links making oneself as nothing with the reception of Torah’s seventy faces.
records.targetEnglish: The beginning of evil’s emergence from hidden potential into an apparent independent existence is pride, which comes from false wisdom, the refuse of true wisdom. Through it a person comes to self-glorification and pride of heart. With true wisdom, the wisdom of Torah, it is otherwise: the more wisdom a person adds, the more humility and lowliness of spirit he adds, as stated in Avot chapter six. Moses our teacher, the teacher of all Israel, was humbler than every person. For all the wisdom of Israel is to recognize that there is none besides Him and that everything comes from God. Consequently, a person recognizes his own lowliness and has nothing of which to boast.
records.explanation: Divrei Soferim explains why humility grows with genuine Torah wisdom. The content of that wisdom is itself the recognition that everything comes from God. This supplies a reason for Rav Tzadok’s claim that the bent, self-effacing ayin receives Torah’s many faces: learning is deepest when it discloses its source and loosens the learner’s claim to independent greatness.

records.themeTitle: Service leads to the recognition of a divine source that precedes service
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok associates becoming as nothing with Atika and the wisdom found from ayin.
records.targetEnglish: The explanation is that there are two kinds of governance through which God conducts His world: the governance of Atika and the governance of Ze’ir Anpin. Ze’ir Anpin indicates what we find that God established: ‘If you seek Him, He will be found by you.’ To the extent that a person seeks, searches and asks after His will, God illuminates for him; as much as a person awakens below, so God illuminates for him above. The governance of Atika indicates that God sometimes conducts matters without needing a person’s service or awakening at all; God illuminates for a person without that person’s awakening. Thus we find in Egypt, ‘You shall be silent,’ and the holy Zohar says, ‘You shall not arouse anything.’ In this place He is not affected by a person’s service at all. Of this place it is said, ‘If you are righteous, what do you give Him?’ In truth God governs through both modes. When a person serves as far as his hand can reach, which is the governance of Ze’ir Anpin, God then shows that Israel’s place is also in that place where the order of service had not yet begun. This indicates that Israel’s place is in Atika. As Tanna Devei Eliyahu says: two things preceded the creation of the world, Torah and Israel. People usually say that Torah came first, but I say Israel came first. After service, God shows Israel that they arose in thought before the order of service began.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains the Atika associated with ayin as the source that precedes a person’s initiative. It preserves a sequence: a person serves to the extent of his capacity, and through that service comes to recognize what was given before his effort. This clarifies how the humility described by Rav Tzadok can accompany serious Torah work. The remainder of Tiferet Yosef explicitly criticizes separating these modes and using the higher source as a reason to abandon service.

records.themeTitle: Torah’s fire becomes stronger through communal learning and a formed teacher
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok calls Torah a fire that consumes the inclination’s fire.
records.targetEnglish: They said, ‘Draw him to the study house,’ rather than simply saying that one should go and study on one’s own. They could also have said, ‘Draw him to words of Torah.’ Although all words of Torah are like fire, it is known that some fire is especially strong, great, and intensely burning, while other fire is small and weak. So it is with the levels of Torah. In the study house, Torah is taught to others, there is the Torah study of the community, and a great person is presumably present. Such Torah acts more powerfully because its fire is stronger. This is the meaning of ‘Therefore those who rule say: Come to Heshbon’: those who rule over their inclination. Only those rulers who have already burned the evil inclination within their bodies through the fire of Torah can act through their words upon the hearts of those who hear them.
records.explanation: Divrei Soferim explains why Torah’s fire can be experienced with different strengths. Communal study and the words of a teacher whose learning has already worked upon his own inclination intensify its effect upon the hearer. This gives a concrete form to the consuming fire described in Pri Tzadik and connects that image to the practice of entering the study house.

records.themeTitle: The measured force taken into holiness deprives destructive anger of its support
records.themeSummary: Jacob wears the goatskins only for a time: Rav Tzadok reads this as the temporary use of scholarly ardor to consume the inclination’s fire.
records.targetEnglish: That is, Israel brought into holiness something of the power of Esau’s angel, so that scholarly anger could be possible among them. From the side of Israel’s own heart, even scholarly anger would not be possible, for their heart is completely free of anger. Only by receiving a small part of the anger of Esau’s angel can scholarly anger exist among them. Esau’s angel thought that he lost nothing by setting aside this power for Israel, since he had no relation to that form of anger: scholarly anger is governed by judgment. It therefore appeared to him to be the very opposite of his own existence, which is only ‘You shall live by your sword,’ without any judgment. In truth he greatly deceived himself. His existence was sustained only as long as that good point remained hidden within his anger. Once that good point was stripped from him, his anger was left without it, because he had handed it over to Israel under the name of scholarly anger. No good aspect remained in his anger, only murder, of which it is said, ‘Only evil all day.’ His entire existence was thereby annulled. Therefore it says concerning him, ‘He shone from Seir to them’: they took from him through shining, an illumination greater than the revealing expressed by hofia, so that his entire existence would be annulled. From Ishmael, the husk of desire, Israel received only through hofia, as explained above in section thirty. They did not annul it entirely; it still requires clarification, and after clarifying it completely they will bring it into holiness. With the husk of Seir, however, once Israel received the point called scholarly anger, no existence remained in it. Anger in itself, apart from scholarly anger, is only what the Talmud describes in Sukkah 52a: the Holy One called it evil. Its existence continues only while desire has not yet been clarified and scholarly anger is still needed. After desire is clarified in the world, even scholarly anger will no longer be needed against it, and that husk will be annulled completely. The attribute of ‘You shall live by your sword’ has no relation to the depth of Israel’s heart; it does not contain even a small point worthy of being brought into holiness.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains both the temporary borrowing of force and its limit. The element brought into holiness is governed by judgment and serves the work of clarification; the destructive anger left behind loses the good that sustained it. The source then says explicitly that even the measured scholarly response ceases to be needed once desire is clarified. This illuminates why Pri Tzadik describes Jacob’s goatskins as a temporary garment rather than his essential character.

records.originEnglish: And on "Capricorn in the year" the Ra'avad cited in his commentary: "And the skins of the kids of the goats she put upon his hands", alluding that goats represent wrath, the root of Esau called "a hairy man (ish sa'ir)"; only temporarily did Rebecca place the goatskins upon the hands of Jacob, an upright man dwelling in tents, so that it serve the purpose of holy rabbinic anger which is like fire, becoming a fire consuming the fire of the Evil Inclination. And this is the meaning of Capricorn in the world: that it be channeled purely within the dimension of holy agitation, which is the zealous fire of Torah words.

records.themeTitle: Joseph’s provision brings holiness into the practical life of the people
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok identifies Joseph’s sustaining his family as the completion of his attribute as the righteous foundation of the world.
records.targetEnglish: Among the souls and powers of action as they unfold into particulars, there are souls whose entire strength is in actual deeds. Their root is Joseph the righteous, ‘who supplied grain to all the people of the land,’ sustaining and providing for them. From his descendants came Joshua, who allotted the land. This is the holiness of bodily deeds that began upon entering the land: this one turns to his olive grove, and so forth, but everything is done in holiness and through the fulfillment of its commandments. Moses our teacher was wholly Torah; therefore he led them in the wilderness, outside settled life and the world of action, a place with no seed, fig, vine or pomegranate, but only the bread that ministering angels eat. Joshua began to clarify the holiness of bodily action: engaging in ordinary worldly activity, with all of it nevertheless in accordance with Torah. ‘Torah together with worldly occupation is good,’ and, ‘If there is no worldly occupation, there is no Torah.’ Worldly occupation is the share of the ordinary people, and it precedes Torah. Torah needs this too: without the leaves, the clusters would not endure. Torah was not given to ministering angels alone, as it was in the wilderness generation. The principal Torah is the study of how to perform commandments, which are bodily actions in this world. Therefore Moses desired to enter the land of Israel to fulfill its commandments, as stated in Sotah 14a.
records.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim explains why feeding and sustaining others completes Joseph’s spiritual role. His power is the root of holiness expressed through practical action, later developed by Joshua in the life of the land. The passage therefore gives content to the move from Joseph’s personal victory over temptation to his sustaining all the tribes: the holiness he preserves becomes provision and action for others.
records.originHebrew: וּבְפָרָשַׁת וַיִּגַּשׁ נֶאֱמַר שֶׁבָּאוּ כָּל הַשְּׁבָטִים וְשִׁבְעִים נֶפֶשׁ, וּכְתִיב: "וַיְכַלְכֵּל יוֹסֵף", וְהוּא שְׁלֵמוּת מִדָּתוֹ שֶׁזָּכָה לִהְיוֹת כַּלְכֹּל וְלִהְיוֹת מֶרְכָּבָה לְמִדַּת צַדִּיק, וְאָז זָכָה לָאוֹר, דִּכְתִיב: "אוֹר זָרֻעַ לַצַּדִּיק".
records.originEnglish: And in Parashat Vayigash it is recorded that all the tribes and seventy souls arrived, and it is written: "And Joseph sustained (vaychalkel)", which is the full perfection of his attribute, meriting to be the universal provider (kalkol) and chariot for Tzaddik, and then he merited the light, as written: "Light is sown for the righteous".

records.themeTitle: Joseph’s additional years refine his relation to suffering itself
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok traces Joseph’s clarification from the trial in Vayeshev through his emergence from prison to kingship in Miketz.
records.targetEnglish: ‘At the end of two full years.’ Joseph was initially in prison for ten years, and afterward two more were added. At first ten were decreed against him because he had sinned against ten tribes. After he was clarified in prison, two more were added, corresponding to himself and Benjamin. This is the measure: when a person sins against God, God brings him into clarifications from which he suffers. After he is clarified for good and receives atonement, he must then suffer over this itself: why did he have to enter a matter that required clarification and suffering? When a person suffers, God, as it were, suffers with him, for ‘In all their affliction, He is afflicted.’ Therefore, after a person clarifies himself according to his sin, he must additionally clarify himself regarding his suffering, for this too contains a trace of sin. As the Talmud explains in Ta’anit 11a, ‘He sinned’ by afflicting himself. Thus ten years were first decreed against Joseph, corresponding to his ten brothers. After he was clarified in prison like silver refined in a furnace, he needed to be clarified regarding his own suffering and that of Benjamin his brother. After he clarified this too during those two years, he was immediately redeemed.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach gives an additional account of what the prolonged clarification involves: sensitivity to the suffering produced by needing correction, including the suffering of another person and, as it were, of God. This expands the prison-to-release stage that Pri Tzadik names briefly. The particular explanation of the ten and two years belongs to Mei HaShiloach; it is not asserted to be Rav Tzadok’s own stated chronology or judgment of Joseph here.
records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 3
records.originHebrew: וְהוּא דְּהִנֵּה בְּפָרָשַׁת וַיֵּשֶׁב כָּל הַפָּרָשָׁה מֵעֵסֶק בֵּרוּר בְּחִינַת צַדִּיק יְסוֹד עוֹלָם, מִדַּת יוֹסֵף (וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ שָׁם), וּבְפָרָשָׁה זוֹ נֶאֱמַר הַתְחָלַת עִנְיַן יוֹסֵף וּבֵרוּר מִדָּתוֹ, וְהַגְּבוּרָה וְהַנִּצּוּחַ לְיֵצֶר הָרָע שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה גִּבּוֹר הַכּוֹבֵשׁ אֶת יִצְרוֹ. וּבְפָרָשַׁת מִקֵּץ הַבֵּרוּר שֶׁלּוֹ שֶׁיָּצָא מִבֵּית הָאֲסוּרִים לִמְלֹךְ.
records.originEnglish: For behold in Parashat Vayeshev the entire portion deals with clarifying the Tzaddik, Foundation of the World, Joseph's attribute (as explained there), and in this portion begins Joseph's narrative and the refinement of his attribute, along with the strength and conquest over the Evil Inclination as he becomes a mighty person who conquers his inclination. And in Parashat Miketz his clarification is that he emerges from prison to reign.

records.themeTitle: Torah itself can enact the purification signified by immersion
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok joins the redirection of anger into Torah’s struggle against the inclination with repair of the covenant.
records.targetEnglish: They abolished the immersion requirement for a person with a seminal emission before Torah study in accordance with Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira, who said, ‘Are not My words like fire?’ This means that words of Torah burn away all evil desires. They also said in Berakhot 16a that tents are compared to streams, and so forth: the words of Torah themselves are analogous to immersion.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik supplies the connection between Torah’s fire and purification of desire that is compressed into the conclusion here. Its preceding discussion develops immersion as a unification of desire, love and awe; it then explains how Torah itself carries out that cleansing. This gives a definite inner meaning to the repair that Rav Tzadok associates with directing the force of agitation against the inclination.

records.themeTitle: Discipline in giving shapes what a person is able to receive
records.themeSummary: Repair of the covenant belongs to the work of bringing one’s powers under God’s will.
records.targetEnglish: ‘Gladness’ is circumcision, as it says, ‘I rejoice over Your word.’ Circumcision is explained in the holy Zohar, Bo 36a: what is the opening of the body? It is circumcision. That is, if a person restrains himself in this place from giving forth except according to God’s will, all his acts of receiving will consequently become clarified as well: he will receive only what accords with God’s will. For when a person’s faculty of giving is clarified, his faculty of receiving is clarified too.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains how the covenant’s discipline reaches beyond a single act. Bringing the power of giving under God’s will forms the corresponding capacity to receive. This illuminates why Pri Tzadik places covenantal repair within the broader work of governing desire and other powers: a clarified boundary changes the person’s whole relation to what enters and leaves his life.
records.originHebrew: וְכֵן חֹדֶשׁ זֶה מְסֻגָּל לְתִקּוּן פְּגַם הַבְּרִית (וְנִתְבָּאֵר לְמַעְלָה), וּכְתִיב: "וְהָסֵר כַּעַס מִלִּבֶּךָ וְהַעֲבֵר רָעָה מִבְּשָׂרֶךָ", וּפְגָם זֶה נִקְרָא "רָע" כַּיָּדוּעַ, וּמְרַמֵּז שֶׁעַל יְדֵי שֶׁיְּתַקֵּן מִדַּת הַכַּעַס, דַּרְגָּא דְּעֵשָׂו, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בִּקְדֻשָּׁה בְּרוֹגֶז שֶׁל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה לְהַרְגִּיז עַל הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע, עַל יְדֵי כֵן יִזְכֶּה לְתַקֵּן פְּגָם זֶה.
records.originEnglish: And so this month is uniquely primed for the repair of the Covenant (explained above), and it is written: "Remove anger from your heart, and put away evil from your flesh", and this blemish is designated "evil" (ra), as is known, alluding that through rectifying the attribute of anger, the level of Esau, channeling it into holiness through the zeal of Torah words to agitate against the Evil Inclination, through this he will merit to rectify this blemish.

records.originHebrew: בְּסֵפֶר יְצִירָה: "הִמְלִיךְ אוֹת עַיִ״ן בְּרֹגֶז וְכוּלֵיהּ, וְטֵבֵת בַּשָּׁנָה" כֵּן הוּא לְגִרְסַת הָאֲרִיזַ"ל; וּלְגִרְסַת הַגְּאוֹנִים (בְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ה׳) בְּחֶשְׁבּוֹן שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר כֹּחוֹת דְּחָשֵׁב שְׂחוֹק עֲשִׂירִי, נִמְצָא לְטֵבֵת אוֹת עַיִ״ן בִּשְׂחוֹק. וּבְוַדַּאי דִּבְרֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם אֱמֶת, שֶׁבְּכָל מַחֲלֹקֶת "אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים"; וּכְבָר אָמַרְנוּ שֶׁיֵּשׁ נְפָשׁוֹת שֶׁאֶצְלָם הַחֹדֶשׁ מְיֻחָד לְעֵסֶק זֶה, וְיֵשׁ נְפָשׁוֹת שֶׁלָּהֶם הַחֹדֶשׁ מְיֻחָד לְעֵסֶק אַחֵר (וְנִתְבָּאֵר רֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ כִּסְלֵו מַאֲמָר ז׳).
records.originEnglish: In Sefer Yetzirah: “He made the letter ayin king over agitation … and Tevet in the year.” This is the Arizal’s reading. In the Geonim’s reading, at the beginning of chapter five, the enumeration of the twelve faculties counts laughter tenth; thus Tevet corresponds to the letter ayin with laughter. Certainly both accounts are true, for in every disagreement “these and those are the words of the living God.” We have already explained that there are souls for whom the month is designated for this form of service, and souls for whom it is designated for another, as explained in Rosh Chodesh Kislev, discourse seven.

records.targetEnglish: As is known, the twelve months correspond to the twelve tribes. Every tribe has a particular excellence and power through which it is distinguished and marked off from the other tribes, and is therefore counted as a tribe in its own right. Although all Israel are “one nation on earth,” truly one, and each person contains all the excellences found in all Israel, a particular excellence becomes manifest especially in the soul corresponding to it. Every matter has world, year, and soul: just as there are differing souls, there are differing times and places. The general division of Israel’s souls into twelve tribes corresponds to the general division of places into the world’s twelve diagonal boundaries, mentioned in Sefer Yetzirah, and the year into twelve months. There are several arrangements of the months and tribes, and great and profound matters are involved in how all these arrangements are true; this awaits another occasion.
records.explanation: Machshavot Charutz explains how distinct monthly assignments can belong to one shared structure. Each soul contains the whole, while a particular power becomes especially manifest in a corresponding soul, time, and place. That distinction between inclusion and manifestation gives substance to Rav Tzadok’s claim here that the differing accounts can each describe the work appropriate to particular souls.

records.targetEnglish: Within Israel too, there are souls permitted to enter uncertainty more than other souls, although both are descendants of Jacob. This is like the matter of Simeon and Dinah. Levi did not wish to take her, for he feared that in the depths his intention might not be for the sake of Heaven. The entire tribe of Levi is characterized by awe and withdrawal from uncertainty, as it is written of them, “I gave them fear,” and so forth. Through this there came from them priests who enter the innermost sanctuary. Their life was therefore clarified immediately, as will be explained in the portion of Korach concerning the staffs. Simeon, however, entered uncertainty and said, “Heaven forbid that I regard myself as an adulterer.” He married Dinah and entered a matter requiring clarification, saying that he trusted God to clarify him for good: his intention was only to take her out of Shechem, and his entire intention was for the sake of Heaven. Therefore the entire tribe of Simeon needed clarification in such matters, as with Zimri, who likewise said that his intention was good, as will be explained in its place. In the future, when the tribe of Simeon is clarified, its level will be greater than Levi’s.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach supplies a concrete account of differentiated spiritual disciplines. Levi’s withdrawal from uncertainty and Simeon’s more exposed path require different kinds of clarification. This helps explain why differing counsel cannot be evaluated independently of the soul receiving it. The source retains the continuing need to test Simeon’s path, including the example of Zimri, and makes the final higher attainment conditional on future clarification.

records.originHebrew: וּלְגִרְסַת הַגְּאוֹנִים: "אוֹת עַיִ״ן בִּשְׂחוֹק", הוּא דִּבֶאֱמֶת אָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת ל״א עַמּוּד א׳): "אָסוּר לְאָדָם שֶׁיְּמַלֵּא שְׂחוֹק פִּיו בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְכוּלֵיהּ", רַק הַפֵּרוּשׁ "בִּשְׂחוֹק" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ בְּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (מְגִלָּה י׳ עַמּוּד ב׳): "הוּא אֵינוֹ שָׂשׂ, אֲבָל אֲחֵרִים מֵשִׂישׂ", שֶׁאַף שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אֵינוֹ שָׂשׂ בְּמַפַּלְתָּן שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים, שֶׁהָיָה רוֹצֶה שֶׁלֹּא יֹאבְדוּ וְיוֹעִיל לָהֶם יִסּוּרִין לְהֵיטִיב דַּרְכָּם, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מוֹעִיל לְיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁשָּׁפְכוּ דָּמָם לִזְכּוֹת לְשִׂמְחָה; וְזֶה אֵינָם זוֹכִים רַק כְּשֶׁזּוֹכִין לְיַשֵּׁר הַלֵּב שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לוֹ שׁוּם נְטִיָּה לָרַע, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (תַּעֲנִית ט״ו עַמּוּד א׳): "יְשָׁרִים לְשִׂמְחָה". וּבַחֲנֻכָּה זָכוּ לְאוֹר תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, וְכֵן הַזְּמַן לִזְכּוֹת בְּכָל חֲנֻכָּה שֶׁיָּאִיר בַּלֵּב אוֹר תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה; וּכְתִיב: "פִּקּוּדֵי הַשֵּׁם יְשָׁרִים מְשַׂמְּחֵי לֵב", שֶׁעַל יְדֵי אוֹר תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה זוֹכִין לְיַשֵּׁר הַלֵּב וּלְשִׂמְחָה.
records.originEnglish: According to the Geonim’s reading, “the letter ayin with laughter”: our Sages indeed said that a person may not fill his mouth with laughter in this world. Rather, “with laughter” has the meaning we explained in the teaching, “He does not rejoice, but causes others to rejoice.” Although God does not rejoice in the downfall of the wicked—He would have wanted them not to perish, and their suffering to help them improve their ways—it nevertheless benefits Israel, whose blood was shed, by bringing them to joy. They attain this only when they attain an upright heart, without any inclination toward evil, as it says, “The upright, for joy.” At Chanukah they attained the light of Oral Torah; likewise, every Chanukah is a time to attain the shining of Oral Torah’s light in the heart. It is written, “The Lord’s precepts are upright, rejoicing the heart”: through the light of Oral Torah, one attains an upright heart and joy.
records.themeTitle: Joy becomes possible through the clarification of the heart
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok distinguishes God’s unwillingness to delight in the destruction of His creatures from the joy granted to Israel, and makes that joy depend on a heart rectified through Torah.
records.targetHebrew: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (ג:) דְּעַל בְּרִיּוֹתָיו אֵינוֹ מְשַׂחֵק אֶלָּא אוֹתוֹ הַיּוֹם. וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בִּמְגִילָּה (י:) דְּאָמַר: "מַעֲשֵׂה יָדַי טוֹבְעִים וְכוּלֵי", וְהוּא אֵינוֹ שָׂשׂ אֲבָל אֲחֵרִים מֵשִׂישׂ. כִּי מִצִּידּוֹ קִילוּסוֹ עוֹלֶה מִן הָרְשָׁעִים, מֵאַחַר שֶׁהֵן גַּם כֵּן בְּרִיּוֹתָיו שֶׁהֲרֵי בּוֹרְאָן וּמְקַיְּימָן בְּכָל יוֹם, וְהִתְלוֹצְצוּת שַׁיָּיךְ רַק מִדָּבָר הַנִּבְדָּל מִמֶּנּוּ וְהוּא מוֹאֵס בּוֹ. וְאֵצֶל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ זֶה, כִּי אִם מוֹאֵס בּוֹ לֹא הָיָה לוֹ שׁוּם קִיּוּם כְּלָל.
records.targetEnglish: Nevertheless, concerning the Holy One they said at the beginning of Avodah Zarah that He does not laugh at His creatures except on that day. This is like the teaching in Megillah: He said, “My handiwork is drowning …”; He does not rejoice, but causes others to rejoice. From His side, His praise rises from the wicked, since they too are His creatures: He creates them and sustains them every day. Mockery applies only to something separate from oneself that one rejects. This does not apply to God, for if He rejected it, it would have no existence at all.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik explains the divine side of the distinction through God’s continuing creation and preservation of those creatures. Derisive laughter entails a separation and rejection that cannot describe His present act of sustaining them. This gives a definite reason for the reluctance to rejoice in their destruction that Pri Tzadik states here; the subsequent discussion in Tzidkat reserves a different condition for the future removal of evil.

records.originHebrew: וּלְגִרְסַת הַגְּאוֹנִים: "אוֹת עַיִ״ן בִּשְׂחוֹק", הוּא דִּבֶאֱמֶת אָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת ל״א עַמּוּד א׳): "אָסוּר לְאָדָם שֶׁיְּמַלֵּא שְׂחוֹק פִּיו בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְכוּלֵיהּ", רַק הַפֵּרוּשׁ "בִּשְׂחוֹק" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ בְּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (מְגִלָּה י׳ עַמּוּד ב׳): "הוּא אֵינוֹ שָׂשׂ, אֲבָל אֲחֵרִים מֵשִׂישׂ", שֶׁאַף שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אֵינוֹ שָׂשׂ בְּמַפַּלְתָּן שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים, שֶׁהָיָה רוֹצֶה שֶׁלֹּא יֹאבְדוּ וְיוֹעִיל לָהֶם יִסּוּרִין לְהֵיטִיב דַּרְכָּם, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מוֹעִיל לְיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁשָּׁפְכוּ דָּמָם לִזְכּוֹת לְשִׂמְחָה; וְזֶה אֵינָם זוֹכִים רַק כְּשֶׁזּוֹכִין לְיַשֵּׁר הַלֵּב שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לוֹ שׁוּם נְטִיָּה לָרַע, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (תַּעֲנִית ט״ו עַמּוּד א׳): "יְשָׁרִים לְשִׂמְחָה". וּבַחֲנֻכָּה זָכוּ לְאוֹר תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, וְכֵן הַזְּמַן לִזְכּוֹת בְּכָל חֲנֻכָּה שֶׁיָּאִיר בַּלֵּב אוֹר תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה; וּכְתִיב: "פִּקּוּדֵי הַשֵּׁם יְשָׁרִים מְשַׂמְּחֵי לֵב", שֶׁעַל יְדֵי אוֹר תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה זוֹכִין לְיַשֵּׁר הַלֵּב וּלְשִׂמְחָה.
records.originEnglish: According to the Geonim’s reading, “the letter ayin with laughter”: our Sages indeed said that a person may not fill his mouth with laughter in this world. Rather, “with laughter” has the meaning we explained in the teaching, “He does not rejoice, but causes others to rejoice.” Although God does not rejoice in the downfall of the wicked—He would have wanted them not to perish, and their suffering to help them improve their ways—it nevertheless benefits Israel, whose blood was shed, by bringing them to joy. They attain this only when they attain an upright heart, without any inclination toward evil, as it says, “The upright, for joy.” At Chanukah they attained the light of Oral Torah; likewise, every Chanukah is a time to attain the shining of Oral Torah’s light in the heart. It is written, “The Lord’s precepts are upright, rejoicing the heart”: through the light of Oral Torah, one attains an upright heart and joy.

records.targetHebrew: וְכֵן הוּא הָעִנְיָן בְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ בְּעֵת שֶׁשָּׁמַע הַבְּשׂוֹרָה כִּי עוֹד יוֹסֵף חַי שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "וַתְּחִי רוּחַ יַעֲקֹב", וְהָיָה יָרֵא לְנַפְשׁוֹ פֶּן הַשִּׂמְחָה הַזֹּאת הִיא רַק שִׂמְחַת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה עַל כֵּן בָּחַן וְצֵירֵף אֶת עַצְמוֹ בְּאֵלּוּ הַבֵּרוּרִים, הַבֵּירֵר הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁאָמַר "אֵלְכָה וְאֶרְאֶנּוּ בְּטֶרֶם אָמוּת", הוּא נֶגֶד לְעוֹלָם יַרְגִּיז אָדָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר, וְהַשֵּׁנִי "וַיִּזְבַּח זְבָחִים לֵאלֹקֵי אָבִיו יִצְחָק", זֶה נֶגֶד יַעֲסוֹק בַּתּוֹרָה כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁמְּבָרְכִין בְּכָל יוֹם אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ לַעֲסוֹק בְּדִבְרֵי תּוֹרָה, כִּי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בִּנְתִינַת הַתּוֹרָה נִקְרָא גְּבוּרָה כָּךְ שָׁמַע מֹשֶׁה מִפִּי הַגְּבוּרָה (מְגִילָּה לָמֶד אָלֶף עַמּוּד בֵּית) כַּיָּדוּעַ לַמֵּבִין, וְשָׁם נֶאֱמַר לוֹ הַמַּאֲמָר "אָנֹכִי אַעַלְךָ גַם עָלֹה" אֲשֶׁר הוּא נֶגֶד הַמַּאֲמָר "אָנֹכִי הַשֵּׁם אֱלֹקֶיךָ אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִיךָ", רַק שָׁם הוּא לֶעָבָר וְהָכָא הוּא לֶעָתִיד, וְגַם מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר "וְאֶת יְהוּדָא שָׁלַח לְפָנָיו" וּפֵירְשׁוּ חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא וַיִּגַּשׁ יוֹד אָלֶף) לְתַקֵּן לוֹ בֵּית תַּלְמוּד הָיָה גַּם כֵּן מֵעִנְיָן הַלָּזֶה, וְאַחַר כָּךְ בֵּירֵר בַּבֵּירֵר הַשְּׁלִישִׁי וַיֵּבְךְּ עַל צַוָּארָיו עוֹד וְדָרְשׁוּ חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה מְלַמֵּד שֶׁקָּרָא קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע, וְאַחַר כָּךְ אָמַר לְיוֹסֵף "אָמוּתָה הַפָּעַם" הוּא נֶגֶד עֵצָה הָרְבִיעִית יַזְכִּיר לוֹ יוֹם הַמִּיתָה, וּכְשֶׁרָאָה יַעֲקֹב כִּי אַחַר כָּל אֵלֶּה נִשְׁאַר לוֹ הַשִּׂמְחָה, אָז הֵבִין כִּי מֵהַשֵּׁם הוּא וְהוּא שִׂמְחָה אֲמִיתִּית וְקַיָּים לָעַד.
records.targetEnglish: This was the matter with Jacob our father when he heard the news that Joseph was still alive, as it says, “The spirit of Jacob revived.” He feared for himself lest this joy be merely a joy of this world, and therefore tested and refined himself through these clarifications. The first clarification was his saying, “I will go and see him before I die,” corresponding to “A person should always stir the good inclination against the evil inclination,” as explained. The second was “He offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac,” corresponding to “He should occupy himself with Torah,” like the blessing we recite each day, “Who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to occupy ourselves with words of Torah.” For in giving the Torah, the Holy One is called Gevurah: “Thus Moses heard from the mouth of the Gevurah,” as is known to the discerning. There Jacob was told, “I will surely bring you up as well,” corresponding to “I am the Lord your God who brought you out”: the latter concerns the past, while the former concerns the future. His sending Judah ahead, which our Sages interpreted as establishing a house of study, also belonged to this matter. He then underwent the third clarification: “He wept upon his neck further,” which our Sages expounded as teaching that he recited the Shema. Afterwards he said to Joseph, “Now I may die,” corresponding to the fourth counsel, to remind himself of the day of death. When Jacob saw that after all these the joy remained, he understood that it came from God and was true joy, enduring forever.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach makes the clarification of joy concrete through Jacob’s response to his reunion with Joseph. Awareness of mortality, Torah, the Shema, and the immediate contemplation of death test what animates his happiness; its persistence through all four allows him to recognize its source. This develops the requirement of an upright heart here without treating the first pleasant feeling as proof that the work is finished.

records.originHebrew: וְהִנֵּה אִיתָא (בְּרָכוֹת ל׳ עַמּוּד ב׳): "חַזְיֵיהּ דַּהֲוָה קָא בָדַח טוּבָא, אָמַר: 'וְגִילוּ בִּרְעָדָה' כְּתִיב; אָמַר לֵיהּ: אֲנָא תְּפִלִּין מַנַּחְנָא וְכוּלֵיהּ", וְלִכְאוֹרָה מַה תֵּרֵץ? הָא אָסוּר לְמַלֵּא שְׂחוֹק פִּיו בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וּכְתִיב: "אָז יִמָּלֵא שְׂחוֹק פִּינוּ", "אָז" דַּוְקָא! אָמְנָם תְּפִלִּין מוֹרֶה שֶׁקְּשׁוּרִים בְּשֹׁרֶשׁ הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה: "בְּרֵאשִׁית" בִּשְׁבִיל יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכוּלֵיהּ, שֶׁכֵּן יִשְׂרָאֵל מַכְתִּירִין בִּפְאֵר הַתְּפִלִּין לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא "הַשֵּׁם אֶחָד", וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מִשְׁתַּבֵּחַ בִּשְׁבָחַיְּהוּ דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב שָׁם ו׳ עַמּוּד א׳); וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְרָאוּ כָּל עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ כִּי שֵׁם הַשֵּׁם נִקְרָא עָלֶיךָ" אֵלּוּ תְּפִלִּין שֶׁבָּרֹאשׁ, "עָלֶיךָ" דַּוְקָא, דִּתְפִלִּין שֶׁל רֹאשׁ הֵם כְּכֶתֶר עַל הָרֹאשׁ. וְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ב׳ נ״ד עַמּוּד א׳): דִּלְשׁוֹן "אָז" מוֹרֶה: כַּד אִתְנְהִיר נְהִירוּ דְּעַתִּיקָא וְכוּלֵיהּ, אָלֶ"ף אַנְקִיב בַּחֲשׁוֹכֵי וְכוּלֵיהּ וּמָטוּ לְזַיִ״ן; א-ז]; וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "אָז יִמָּלֵא שְׂחוֹק פִּינוּ", דִּלְעָתִיד יִתְגַּלֶּה וְיָאִיר בְּחִינַת "הוּא", שֶׁעַל שֵׁם זֶה נִקְרָא "בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא", שֶׁיָּאִיר כְּיוֹם בְּחִינַת הוּ"א שֶׁמּוֹרֶה עַתִּיקָא כַּיָּדוּעַ, וְזֶהוּ אָ"ז דַּוְקָא "יִמָּלֵא שְׂחוֹק פִּינוּ". וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר: "אֲנָא תְּפִלִּין מַנַּחְנָא", שֶׁבְּשָׁעָה שֶׁהַיִּשְׂרָאֵל מַנִּיחַ תְּפִלִּין מוֹפִיעַ בּוֹ הִתְגַּלּוּת מֵאוֹר עַתִּיקָא שֶׁקָּשׁוּר בַּשֹּׁרֶשׁ, וְהוּא גַּם כֵּן אָ"ז כָּאָמוּר.
records.originEnglish: The Talmud relates that he saw his colleague being especially cheerful and said, “It is written, ‘Rejoice with trembling.’” He replied, “I am wearing tefillin.” What did this answer? One may not fill one’s mouth with laughter in this world, and it is written, “Then our mouth will be filled with laughter”—specifically then! Tefillin indicate attachment to the root of thought: “In the beginning”—for the sake of Israel. Israel crown the Holy One with the splendor of tefillin, proclaiming “The Lord is one,” and the Holy One praises Israel’s excellence. Thus “all the peoples of the earth will see that the Lord’s name is called upon you” refers to the tefillin of the head. “Upon you” is precise: the head tefillin are like a crown upon the head. The Zohar explains that the word az, “then,” indicates the illumination of Atika: the alef pierces the darkness and reaches the zayin—alef-zayin. This is “Then our mouth will be filled with laughter.” In the future the aspect signified by “He” will be disclosed and illuminate; hence “on that day,” when the aspect called “He,” indicating Atika, will shine like day. Specifically then our mouth will be filled with laughter. This is the answer, “I am wearing tefillin”: when a Jew puts on tefillin, a disclosure of Atika’s light shines within him through his attachment to the root. This too is “then.”
records.themeTitle: Tefillin allow a present taste of the future disclosure
records.themeSummary: The answer “I am wearing tefillin” identifies a moment when the hidden root becomes illuminated, making the future “then” present within a mitzvah.
records.targetHebrew: וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ: לְאָדָם שֶׁטּוֹב מַטְעִימִין לוֹ מִפְּרִי מַעֲשָׂיו בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, הַיְנוּ שֶׁלִּפְרָקִים הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר לָאָדָם וּמַתְחִיל לְהִתְלַהֵב לִבּוֹ וּמַמָּשׁ מַרְגִּישׁ חַיּוּת בַּלֵּב וְנַפְשׁוֹ תָּגִיל בַּה' שֶׁעִקַּר הַחַיּוּת הִיא הַשִּׂמְחָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּזֹהַר סוֹף פָּרָשַׁת וַיַּקְהֵל שָׁם עַל "בְּעֶצֶב" דְּהַיְנוּ הַמִּיתָה, וּבְשַׁבָּת שֶׁמֵּעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא דָּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה ק׳ פִּסְקָא ז׳): "וְלֹא יוֹסִף עֶצֶב עִמָּהּ" — זֶה הָאֵבֶל וְלָכֵן נֶאֱמַר בְּשַׁבָּת: "וְהִתְעַנַּג עַל ה'", וְדָרְשׁוּ בַּזֹּהַר "עַל" מַמָּשׁ, דְּהוּא סְעוּדָתָא דְּעַתִּיקָא קַדִּישָׁא, פֵּרוּשׁ: כִּי שֵׁם הֲוָיָ"ה הַיְנוּ הַרְגָּשַׁת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נֹכַח עֵינָיו וְהוּא בְּהַגְדָּרַת הַתּוֹרָה אֲבָל בְּשַׁבָּת יָכוֹל לְהִתְעַנֵּג בְּהַרְחָבָה וּלְמַעְלָה מִדַּרְגָּא דְּהַשָּׂגַת שֵׁם הֲוָיָ"ה רַק בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת כְּטֶבַע הַשִּׂמְחָה שֶׁמִּצִּדָּהּ הוּא הַהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת וְהַעֲבָרַת טֶבַע הַהַגְדָּרָה מִצַּד הַרְחָבַת הַלֵּב וְהַיְנוּ כִּי הִיא סְעוּדָתָא דְּעַתִּיקָא קַדִּישָׁא, פֵּרוּשׁ: הַשִּׂמְחָה שֶׁאָנוּ עוֹשִׂין מִצַּד דְּבֵקוּתֵנוּ בַּשֹּׁרֶשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם, שֶׁזֶּהוּ מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת תַּעֲנוּגִים אַף מַה שֶּׁנִּרְאֶה לְגַרְמֵיהּ הַכֹּל לִכְבוֹד שָׁמַיִם מֵאַחַר שֶׁדָּבוּק בַּשֹּׁרֶשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק אֵין עוֹמְדִין (בְּרָכוֹת דַּף ל׳ עַמּוּד ב׳) חַזְיֵיהּ דְּקָא בָדַח טוּבָא, אֲמַר לֵיהּ: תְּפִלִּין מַנַּחְנָא, פֵּרוּשׁ: דְּקַרְקַפְתָּא דִּמְנַח תְּפִלִּין הַיְנוּ הַדְּבֵקוּת בַּשֹּׁרֶשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר לְעֵיל [וְכִדְאִיתָא בַּתִּקּוּנִים וּמַאֲמַר פָּתַח אֵלִיָּהוּ], מִצִּדּוֹ הִיא הַשִּׂמְחָה הַגְּדוֹלָה וְלָכֵן נִקְרָא תְּפִלִּין "אוֹת" וְכֵן שַׁבָּת, דִּשְׁנֵיהֶם אוֹת אַשֹּׁרֶשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם שֶׁהוּא הַהַבְדָּלָה בֵּין יִשְׂרָאֵל לְעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת [כְּמוֹ אוֹת הַבְּרִית]
records.targetEnglish: Therefore they said that a good person is given a taste of the fruit of his deeds in this world: at intervals God illuminates for a person, his heart begins to burn with enthusiasm, and he actually feels life in his heart, while his soul rejoices in God. For the essence of life is joy, as explained in the Zohar at the end of Vayakhel concerning “in sorrow,” which signifies death. Of Shabbat, which is a taste of the World to Come, our Sages expounded in Bereshit Rabbah, “‘He adds no sorrow with it’—this is the mourner.” Therefore on Shabbat it says, “Delight in the Lord,” and the Zohar reads “in” as literally “above”: it is the meal of Atika Kadisha. The divine name indicates sensing God before one’s eyes, within the defined form of Torah. On Shabbat, however, a person can delight expansively, above that level of apprehension, with the expansiveness of joy that carries one beyond the usual boundaries through the heart’s widening. This is the meal of Atika Kadisha: the joy we experience through attachment to the hidden root, a taste of the World to Come in the expansion of delights. Even what appears directed toward oneself is all for the honor of Heaven, since one is attached to the hidden root. Thus at the beginning of the chapter Ein Omdin, when he saw his colleague being especially cheerful, the reply was, “I am wearing tefillin.” The head that bears tefillin signifies attachment to the hidden root, as explained above and in the Tikkunim’s Patach Eliyahu; from this comes the great joy. Therefore tefillin are called a sign, as is Shabbat: both signify the hidden root that distinguishes Israel from idolaters, like the sign of the covenant.
records.explanation: Dover Tzedek explains what this anticipated future can mean within present experience: life already given to the heart becomes actively felt, and that awakening brings joy. Its discussion of Shabbat and tefillin supplies the experiential content of attachment to the hidden root. This develops Pri Tzadik’s answer by showing how an otherwise future disclosure can be tasted at a particular moment in this world.

records.originHebrew: וְהִנֵּה אִיתָא (בְּרָכוֹת ל׳ עַמּוּד ב׳): "חַזְיֵיהּ דַּהֲוָה קָא בָדַח טוּבָא, אָמַר: 'וְגִילוּ בִּרְעָדָה' כְּתִיב; אָמַר לֵיהּ: אֲנָא תְּפִלִּין מַנַּחְנָא וְכוּלֵיהּ", וְלִכְאוֹרָה מַה תֵּרֵץ? הָא אָסוּר לְמַלֵּא שְׂחוֹק פִּיו בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וּכְתִיב: "אָז יִמָּלֵא שְׂחוֹק פִּינוּ", "אָז" דַּוְקָא! אָמְנָם תְּפִלִּין מוֹרֶה שֶׁקְּשׁוּרִים בְּשֹׁרֶשׁ הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה: "בְּרֵאשִׁית" בִּשְׁבִיל יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכוּלֵיהּ, שֶׁכֵּן יִשְׂרָאֵל מַכְתִּירִין בִּפְאֵר הַתְּפִלִּין לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא "הַשֵּׁם אֶחָד", וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מִשְׁתַּבֵּחַ בִּשְׁבָחַיְּהוּ דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב שָׁם ו׳ עַמּוּד א׳); וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְרָאוּ כָּל עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ כִּי שֵׁם הַשֵּׁם נִקְרָא עָלֶיךָ" אֵלּוּ תְּפִלִּין שֶׁבָּרֹאשׁ, "עָלֶיךָ" דַּוְקָא, דִּתְפִלִּין שֶׁל רֹאשׁ הֵם כְּכֶתֶר עַל הָרֹאשׁ. וְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ב׳ נ״ד עַמּוּד א׳): דִּלְשׁוֹן "אָז" מוֹרֶה: כַּד אִתְנְהִיר נְהִירוּ דְּעַתִּיקָא וְכוּלֵיהּ, אָלֶ"ף אַנְקִיב בַּחֲשׁוֹכֵי וְכוּלֵיהּ וּמָטוּ לְזַיִ״ן; א-ז]; וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "אָז יִמָּלֵא שְׂחוֹק פִּינוּ", דִּלְעָתִיד יִתְגַּלֶּה וְיָאִיר בְּחִינַת "הוּא", שֶׁעַל שֵׁם זֶה נִקְרָא "בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא", שֶׁיָּאִיר כְּיוֹם בְּחִינַת הוּ"א שֶׁמּוֹרֶה עַתִּיקָא כַּיָּדוּעַ, וְזֶהוּ אָ"ז דַּוְקָא "יִמָּלֵא שְׂחוֹק פִּינוּ". וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר: "אֲנָא תְּפִלִּין מַנַּחְנָא", שֶׁבְּשָׁעָה שֶׁהַיִּשְׂרָאֵל מַנִּיחַ תְּפִלִּין מוֹפִיעַ בּוֹ הִתְגַּלּוּת מֵאוֹר עַתִּיקָא שֶׁקָּשׁוּר בַּשֹּׁרֶשׁ, וְהוּא גַּם כֵּן אָ"ז כָּאָמוּר.
records.originEnglish: The Talmud relates that he saw his colleague being especially cheerful and said, “It is written, ‘Rejoice with trembling.’” He replied, “I am wearing tefillin.” What did this answer? One may not fill one’s mouth with laughter in this world, and it is written, “Then our mouth will be filled with laughter”—specifically then! Tefillin indicate attachment to the root of thought: “In the beginning”—for the sake of Israel. Israel crown the Holy One with the splendor of tefillin, proclaiming “The Lord is one,” and the Holy One praises Israel’s excellence. Thus “all the peoples of the earth will see that the Lord’s name is called upon you” refers to the tefillin of the head. “Upon you” is precise: the head tefillin are like a crown upon the head. The Zohar explains that the word az, “then,” indicates the illumination of Atika: the alef pierces the darkness and reaches the zayin—alef-zayin. This is “Then our mouth will be filled with laughter.” In the future the aspect signified by “He” will be disclosed and illuminate; hence “on that day,” when the aspect called “He,” indicating Atika, will shine like day. Specifically then our mouth will be filled with laughter. This is the answer, “I am wearing tefillin”: when a Jew puts on tefillin, a disclosure of Atika’s light shines within him through his attachment to the root. This too is “then.”

records.targetHebrew: ויקר אלו תפילין וכו'. כי בתפילין דמארי עלמא מה כתיב כי מי גוי גדול ומי גוי גדול כדאיתא בגמ' (ברכות ו.) היינו כי תפילין הוא לבוש לאורו ית' שאור רצונו ית' נתלבש בזאת המצוה וכשאדם מניח אותם עי"ז יכול להשיג את אורו ית' המלובש בהם ומרמזין על כל פעולות המצות שיכול האדם לחפור בהם ולגלות את האור השוכן בהם.
records.targetEnglish: “Honor”—these are tefillin. For what is written in the Master of the world’s tefillin? “Who is a great nation,” and “Who is a great nation,” as the Talmud states in Berakhot 6a. Tefillin are a garment for His light: the light of His will is clothed in this mitzvah, and when a person puts them on he can thereby attain the divine light clothed within them. They allude to all the acts of the commandments, in which a person can dig and disclose the light dwelling within them.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains how the physical mitzvah can carry the disclosure described here. Tefillin clothe the light of God’s will in a form that becomes accessible through actually performing the commandment. The hidden root is thus received through a concrete act. The complete Purim paragraph keeps this within its requirement of service amid concealment before the unity of the hidden and revealed modes is disclosed.
