records.originHebrew: וּבְחִבּוּר חָכְמָה שֶׁבַּמֹּחַ עִם בִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב זוֹכִין לִבְחִינַת הַדַּעַת, וּכְמַה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "כִּי תָבוֹא חָכְמָה בְלִבֶּךָ וְדַעַת לְנַפְשְׁךָ יִנְעָם". וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרְאוּ הַסַּנְהֶדְרִין "עֵינֵי הָעֵדָה" וְכֵן כָּל הַחֲכָמִים, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא ד׳ עַמּוּד א׳) בְּהוֹרְדוֹס: "הוּא סִמֵּא עֵינוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם", כִּי שֹׁרֶשׁ תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה מֵהַדַּעַת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים. וּלְהִתְגַּלּוּת אוֹר זֶה זוֹכִין רַק יְרֵאִים וְצַדִּיקִים, וְעַל זֶה רוֹמֵז מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "הִנֵּה עֵין הַשֵּׁם אֶל יְרֵאָיו", וְנֶאֱמַר: "עֵינֵי הַשֵּׁם אֶל צַדִּיקִים", שֶׁהַצַּדִּיק וְהַיָּרֵא זוֹכֶה לִבְחִינַת עֵין הַשֵּׁם שֶׁהוּא הַדַּעַת. וּכְתִיב: "אוֹר זָרֻעַ לַצַּדִּיק", וּכְתִיב: "אוֹר צַדִּיקִים יִשְׂמָח", שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הָאוֹר שֶׁזּוֹכֶה הַצַּדִּיק זוֹכֶה לְיַשֵּׁר הַלֵּב שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לוֹ שׁוּם נְטִיָּה לָרַע, וּלְ"יִשְׁרֵי לֵב שִׂמְחָה". וְזֶה עַל יְדֵי שֶׁזּוֹכֶה לִבְחִינַת הַדַּעַת שֶׁהוּא פְּנִימִיּוּת הַכֶּתֶר כַּיָּדוּעַ; וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר: "הִמְלִיךְ אוֹת עַיִ״ן בִּשְׂחוֹק", שֶׁאָז מוֹפִיעַ בּוֹ מֵעֵין הֶעָתִיד.
records.originEnglish: Through the joining of wisdom in the mind with understanding in the heart, one attains knowledge, as it says, “For wisdom will enter your heart, and knowledge will be pleasant to your soul.” Therefore the Sanhedrin, and likewise all the sages, are called “the eyes of the congregation”; concerning Herod they said, “He blinded the eye of the world.” For the root of Oral Torah is knowledge, as we have often explained. Only those who fear God and the righteous attain the disclosure of this light. This is alluded to by “The Lord’s eye is upon those who fear Him,” and “The Lord’s eyes are toward the righteous.” The righteous person who fears God attains the aspect of the Lord’s eye, which is knowledge. It is written, “Light is sown for the righteous,” and “The light of the righteous rejoices”: through the light he attains, the righteous person attains an upright heart, without any inclination toward evil, and “joy for the upright of heart.” This occurs through attaining knowledge, which is the inwardness of the crown, as is known. This is “He made the letter ayin king over laughter”: a taste of the future then shines within him.
records.themeTitle: Knowledge joins the mind and heart so that Torah becomes lived joy
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok traces a sequence from wisdom entering the heart to knowledge, the light of Oral Torah, an upright heart, and joy.
records.targetHebrew: וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הוּא הַדַּעַת הַמְחַבֵּר חָכְמָה וּבִינָה, שֶׁהֵם מוֹחָא וְלִבָּא. זֶהוּ עִנְיַן הַתּוֹרָה, לְשׁוֹן הוֹרָאָה, שֶׁמּוֹרָה הַלֵּב לִהְיוֹת נִמְשָׁךְ אַחַר הַחָכְמָה שֶׁל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ; דְּזוּלַת זֶה, כְּשֶׁאֵין מוֹרֶה לַלֵּב, אֵינוֹ נִקְרָא "תּוֹרָה" אֶלָּא "חָכְמָה" לְבַד. וְזֶה כֹּחַ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁבָּא וְהוֹרִיד הַתּוֹרָה לָאָרֶץ וְהִנְחִילָהּ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ כֹּחַ זֶה לִהְיוֹת הַלֵּב נִמְשָׁךְ אַחַר חָכְמַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ. אֲבָל אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם אֵין לָהֶם שַׁיָּכוּת לָזֶה. וּבִלְעָם, שֶׁהָיָה נֶגֶד זֶה, הִתְפָּאֵר "וְיֹדֵעַ דַּעַת עֶלְיוֹן": שֶׁהָיָה יוֹדֵעַ וּמַשִּׂיג דַּרְגָא דְּדַעַת זוֹ, אֶלָּא שֶׁקְּרָאָהּ "דַּעַת עֶלְיוֹן" — פֵּרוּשׁ, עֶלְיוֹן מַה שֶּׁהוּא לְמַעְלָה מִמַּדְרֵגַת מוֹחוֹ וְלִבּוֹ, דְּאֶצְלוֹ הָיָה זֶה לְמַעְלָה מִן הַטֶּבַע. וְהַיְנוּ, אַף שֶׁהוּא גַּם כֵּן הָיָה יוֹדֵעַ רִבּוֹנוֹ וּמִתְנַהֵג גַּם כֵּן בְּדֶרֶךְ הַתּוֹרָה בִּשְׁמִירָה מִקִּנְאָה, תַּאֲוָה וְכָבוֹד, בֶּאֱמֶת הָיָה מְשֻׁקָּע בָּהֶם כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּרֵר אָז בְּאוֹתוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה, שֶׁהָיוּ לוֹ כָּל שָׁלֹשׁ מִדּוֹת רָעוֹת בֶּאֱמֶת בְּמַעֲמַקֵּי לִבּוֹ.
records.targetEnglish: Moses our teacher is the knowledge that joins wisdom and understanding, which are mind and heart. This is the meaning of Torah, from the word instruction: it instructs the heart to follow God’s wisdom. Without this, when it does not instruct the heart, it is called only wisdom, not Torah. This is Moses’ power: he brought Torah down to earth and bequeathed it to Israel, possessing the power to make the heart follow God’s wisdom. The nations do not have a share in this. Balaam, who corresponded to him in opposition, boasted that he “knows the knowledge of the Most High.” He knew and apprehended this level of knowledge, but called it “knowledge of the Most High,” meaning that it was above the level of his own mind and heart: for him it was above nature. Although he too knew his Master and outwardly conducted himself according to Torah, guarding against jealousy, desire, and honor, in truth he was immersed in them, as explained above. That very incident clarified that he actually possessed all three bad traits in the depths of his heart.
records.explanation: Resisei Layla explains what the joining of mind and heart accomplishes. Knowledge becomes Torah when it directs the heart in accordance with the wisdom it apprehends; Balaam illustrates the separation between knowing a truth and having one’s inner traits formed by it. This makes the sequence in Pri Tzadik intelligible: the knowledge that leads to joy includes the rectification of the heart, beyond intellectual apprehension alone.

records.originHebrew: וּבְחִבּוּר חָכְמָה שֶׁבַּמֹּחַ עִם בִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב זוֹכִין לִבְחִינַת הַדַּעַת, וּכְמַה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "כִּי תָבוֹא חָכְמָה בְלִבֶּךָ וְדַעַת לְנַפְשְׁךָ יִנְעָם". וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרְאוּ הַסַּנְהֶדְרִין "עֵינֵי הָעֵדָה" וְכֵן כָּל הַחֲכָמִים, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא ד׳ עַמּוּד א׳) בְּהוֹרְדוֹס: "הוּא סִמֵּא עֵינוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם", כִּי שֹׁרֶשׁ תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה מֵהַדַּעַת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים. וּלְהִתְגַּלּוּת אוֹר זֶה זוֹכִין רַק יְרֵאִים וְצַדִּיקִים, וְעַל זֶה רוֹמֵז מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "הִנֵּה עֵין הַשֵּׁם אֶל יְרֵאָיו", וְנֶאֱמַר: "עֵינֵי הַשֵּׁם אֶל צַדִּיקִים", שֶׁהַצַּדִּיק וְהַיָּרֵא זוֹכֶה לִבְחִינַת עֵין הַשֵּׁם שֶׁהוּא הַדַּעַת. וּכְתִיב: "אוֹר זָרֻעַ לַצַּדִּיק", וּכְתִיב: "אוֹר צַדִּיקִים יִשְׂמָח", שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הָאוֹר שֶׁזּוֹכֶה הַצַּדִּיק זוֹכֶה לְיַשֵּׁר הַלֵּב שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לוֹ שׁוּם נְטִיָּה לָרַע, וּלְ"יִשְׁרֵי לֵב שִׂמְחָה". וְזֶה עַל יְדֵי שֶׁזּוֹכֶה לִבְחִינַת הַדַּעַת שֶׁהוּא פְּנִימִיּוּת הַכֶּתֶר כַּיָּדוּעַ; וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר: "הִמְלִיךְ אוֹת עַיִ״ן בִּשְׂחוֹק", שֶׁאָז מוֹפִיעַ בּוֹ מֵעֵין הֶעָתִיד.
records.originEnglish: Through the joining of wisdom in the mind with understanding in the heart, one attains knowledge, as it says, “For wisdom will enter your heart, and knowledge will be pleasant to your soul.” Therefore the Sanhedrin, and likewise all the sages, are called “the eyes of the congregation”; concerning Herod they said, “He blinded the eye of the world.” For the root of Oral Torah is knowledge, as we have often explained. Only those who fear God and the righteous attain the disclosure of this light. This is alluded to by “The Lord’s eye is upon those who fear Him,” and “The Lord’s eyes are toward the righteous.” The righteous person who fears God attains the aspect of the Lord’s eye, which is knowledge. It is written, “Light is sown for the righteous,” and “The light of the righteous rejoices”: through the light he attains, the righteous person attains an upright heart, without any inclination toward evil, and “joy for the upright of heart.” This occurs through attaining knowledge, which is the inwardness of the crown, as is known. This is “He made the letter ayin king over laughter”: a taste of the future then shines within him.

records.targetHebrew: כי ענין שמחה, ביאר אזמו"ר הגה"ק זללה"ה, שנתעורר בלב עיקר השמחה בשעה שהאדם עומד בבהירות ומכיר איך שהכל הוא ביד השי"ת, ע"ד הכתוב (דברי הימים א כ״ט:י״ד) כי ממך הכל ומידך נתנו לך, היינו שמכיר שגם זאת הדיעה צלולה למסור בחזרה להשי"ת, גם זאת הנדיבות הוא נמי מהשי"ת, מה שאין שמחה כזו גבי שום אומה ולשון. כי עליהם נאמר (חבקוק ב׳:ד׳) הנה עפלה לא ישרה נפשו בו, היינו אף שיש להם כל הטובות מ"מ אין בלבבם שום נייחא ושמחה. כי עיקר הנייחא והשמחה הוא רק בדיעה, וכשמכיר האדם שזאת הדיעה צלולה הוא נמי רק שהשי"ת חנן אותו בדיעה צלולה כזו, מזה נתרבה בנפשו עוז בגודל שמחה, כמו שמצינו (דברי הימים א כ״ט:ט׳) וישמחו העם על התנדבם כי בלב שלם התנדבו לד' וגו', היינו ששמחו מזה בעצמו שחנן להם השי"ת בדיעה צלולה על זאת הנדיבות.
records.targetEnglish: Regarding joy, my holy grandfather explained that its essence awakens in the heart when a person stands in clarity and recognizes that everything is in God’s hands, as it says, “Everything is from You, and from Your hand we have given to You.” One recognizes that even this clear awareness through which one gives back to God, and even this generosity, also come from God. No nation or language has joy like this. Concerning them it says, “Behold, his soul is swollen; it is not upright within him”: even when they possess every good, they have no rest or joy in their hearts. For the essence of rest and joy is in awareness. When a person recognizes that this clear awareness too comes only from God, who graced him with such clarity, strength increases in his soul with great joy. Thus we find, “The people rejoiced over their voluntary giving, for with a whole heart they gave willingly to the Lord”: they rejoiced over this itself, that God had graced them with clear awareness concerning their generosity.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains why clear knowledge can generate joy in the heart: one recognizes both the received good and the ability to recognize and return it as gifts from God. Its example of wholehearted voluntary giving makes that inward knowledge visible in action. This adds content to Pri Tzadik’s movement from knowledge to an upright and joyful heart, while keeping joy grounded in its divine source.

records.originHebrew: וְהָעִקָּר מִצַּד הָאָדָם: "הִמְלִיךְ אוֹת עַיִ״ן בְּרֹגֶז", לְהַרְגִּיז יֵצֶר טוֹב עַל יֵצֶר הָרָע, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה זוֹכֶה לִבְחִינַת צַדִּיק, דִּכְתִיב: "עֵינֵי הַשֵּׁם אֶל צַדִּיקִים", שֶׁבַּהֲפָכָה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם נִקְרָא "רַע בְּעֵינֵי הַשֵּׁם" וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ. וְעַל יְדֵי מַה שֶּׁמַּרְגִּיז הַיֵּצֶר טוֹב עַל יֵצֶר הָרָע זוֹכִין לִבְחִינַת שְׂחוֹק, שֶׁזּוֹכִין לְיַשֵּׁר הַלֵּב. וְזֶה זָכוּ בַּחֲנֻכָּה כְּשֶׁכָּבְשׁוּ קְלִפַּת יָוָן וְזָכוּ לָאוֹר, וַ"אֲחֵרִים מֵשִׂישׂ", שֶׁזָּכוּ לְ"יִשְׁרֵי לֵב שִׂמְחָה", וְזֶה עֵסֶק חֹדֶשׁ טֵבֵת שֶׁרֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ שֶׁלּוֹ חָל בַּחֲנֻכָּה.
records.originEnglish: The principal work from the person’s side is “He made the letter ayin king over agitation”: to stir the good inclination against the evil inclination. Through this one attains the quality of the righteous, of whom it is written, “The Lord’s eyes are toward the righteous”; its opposite, God forbid, is called “evil in the Lord’s eyes,” as we have explained. Through stirring the good inclination against the evil inclination, one attains the quality of laughter, by attaining an upright heart. This is what they attained at Chanukah when they conquered the husk of Greece and merited light, and “He causes others to rejoice”: they attained “joy for the upright of heart.” This is the work of Tevet, whose Rosh Chodesh falls during Chanukah.
records.themeTitle: The person’s work of awe prepares the heart’s later expansiveness
records.themeSummary: The conclusion joins the two readings in a sequence: a person undertakes the struggle against the inclination, and through it attains the upright heart that can rejoice.
records.targetHebrew: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם, צָרִיךְ לִטְרוֹחַ בְּבִישּׁוּל הַמַּאֲכָלִים בְּעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת; אֲבָל מִי שֶׁלֹּא טָרַח בְּעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת מַה יֹּאכַל בְּשַׁבָּת? כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ד עַמּוּד ב; ג.: דְּבָרִים ז, יא "הַיּוֹם לַעֲשׂוֹתָם" – וּמָחָר לְקַבֵּל שְׂכָרָם; שֶׁאֵינוֹ בָּא מֵעַצְמוֹ אוֹר הַזֶּה לָאָדָם. וְכֵן נֵר שַׁבָּת צָרִיךְ לְהַדְלִיק מֵעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת, אֲבָל בְּשַׁבָּת אֵין עוֹד זְמַן לְעוֹרֵר הַיִּרְאָה אָז, כִּי כֻּלּוֹ אַהֲבָה וּדְבֵיקוּת בַּה', וְהַדְלָקַת הַנֵּר סְמוּכָה לְשַׁבָּת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שַׁבָּת לה:: בִּלְבַד שֶׁלֹּא יַקְדִּים וְכוּלֵי; כְּעִנְיַן חֶבְלֵי מָשִׁיחַ הַסְּמוּכִים בְּעִקְבְתָא דִּמְשִׁיחָא, כִּי לְעוֹלָם הַדְּבֵיקוּת וְאַהֲבָה תְּכוּפָה אַחַר הַיִּרְאָה.
records.targetEnglish: Nevertheless, one must labor over cooking the food before Shabbat. One who did not labor before Shabbat—what will he eat on Shabbat? As stated at the beginning of Avodah Zarah, “Today, to do them”—and tomorrow to receive their reward: this light does not come to a person by itself. Likewise, the Shabbat lamp must be lit before Shabbat. On Shabbat it is no longer the time to awaken awe, for it is entirely love and attachment to God. The lamp is lit close to Shabbat, “provided he does not do so too early,” and so forth. This is like the birth pangs of the Messiah, which come close to his arrival, for attachment and love always follow closely after awe.
records.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah explains the relation through preparation for Shabbat. The expansive light of rest is received through earlier work, and the last preparation of awe stands directly beside the love that follows. This develops the conclusion of Pri Tzadik: agitation is the person’s preparatory work, while the joy that follows is the fruit of a heart made ready to receive the light.

records.originHebrew: "הַנֵּרוֹת הַלָּלוּ וְכוּלֵיהּ אֶלָּא לִרְאוֹתָן בִּלְבָד, כְּדֵי לְהוֹדוֹת וְכוּלֵיהּ": הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "פִּתְחוּ לִי שַׁעֲרֵי צֶדֶק, אָבֹא בָם אוֹדֶה יָהּ; זֶה הַשַּׁעַר לַהשֵּׁם וְגוֹמֵר", כִּי כַּאֲשֶׁר זוֹכִים לִהְיוֹת נִפְתָּחִים בַּלֵּב הַשַּׁעֲרֵי צֶדֶק עַל יְדֵי הוֹפָעַת הִתְגַּלּוּת כְּבוֹד מַלְכוּתוֹ, עַל יְדֵי זֶה בָּאִים לְהוֹדוֹת וּלְהַלֵּל לַהשֵּׁם, כְּעִנְיַן מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "אֲדֹנָי שְׂפָתַי תִּפְתָּח" וְהַיְנוּ הַשַּׁעֲרֵי צֶדֶק, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה: "וּפִי יַגִּיד תְּהִלָּתֶךָ". וּבַמֶּה זוֹכִים לָזֶה? עַל זֶה אָמַר: "זֶה הַשַּׁעַר לַהשֵּׁם, צַדִּיקִים יָבֹאוּ בוֹ" עַל יְדֵי הַתִּקּוּן קְדֻשַּׁת הַבְּרִית שֶׁהוּא בְּחִינַת צַדִּיק, זוֹכִין לְהֶאָרַת שַׁעֲרֵי צֶדֶק בַּלֵּב, כְּמַה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "אוֹר זָרֻעַ לַצַּדִּיק", וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה בָּאִים לְהוֹדוֹת וּלְהַלֵּל.
records.originEnglish: “These lights … we may do nothing with them except look at them, in order to give thanks …”: this follows what is written, “Open for me the gates of righteousness; I shall enter them and thank Yah. This is the gate of the Lord ….” When a person merits having the gates of righteousness opened in the heart through the shining revelation of the glory of His kingship, this brings thanksgiving and praise to God. It is like “My Lord, open my lips”—these are the gates of righteousness—and thereby “my mouth will declare Your praise.” How does one merit this? The verse says, “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous enter it.” Through the repair of the holiness of the covenant, which is the quality of the righteous one, a person merits the illumination of the gates of righteousness within the heart, as it says, “Light is sown for the righteous.” Through this one comes to give thanks and praise.

records.targetHebrew: ולכן בשבת כשמדבר האדם והוא בחינת פי ה' מועיל הדברים שיכנסו ללב ולבבו יבין ושב ומש"ה כתיב טוב להודות לה' שעל ידי ההודאה בעצמה יזכה שיכנס ללב ויהיה מודה ועוזב ויהיה בכלל ועמך כולם צדיקים שיוכל לבא בשערי צדק השער שצדיקים יבאו בו.
records.targetEnglish: Therefore, on Shabbat, when a person speaks and the speech is in the quality of “the mouth of the Lord,” the words are effective in entering the heart, so that “his heart will understand and he will return.” That is why it says, “It is good to give thanks to the Lord”: through the thanksgiving itself a person merits its entering the heart, becoming one who “confesses and abandons” wrongdoing, and being included in “Your people are all righteous.” One can then enter the gates of righteousness, the gate that the righteous enter.
records.explanation: The Matot teaching explains the inward effectiveness of the thanksgiving described here. In its particular Shabbat setting, spoken thanks can enter the heart and lead to abandoning wrongdoing, opening the very gates of righteousness named in Chanukah 20. This gives the reader a concrete account of how praise and an opened heart can strengthen one another; it does not transfer Shabbat’s special efficacy automatically to every occasion.

records.targetHebrew: אמרו לפני זכרונות היינו כ"ד במדרש אנו שכחה מצוי בינינו רק ע"י שישראל מצמצמים א"ע ומבטלים כל הרצונות מבלי לחפוץ כי אם רצונו ית' ואומרים קודם בקשת תפלתם אדני שפתי תפתח להורות שאינם מבקשים רק מה שהוא רצונו ית' וזהו אמרו לפני זכרונות כדי שיעלה זכרוניכם לפני לטובה היינו כדי שאראה לכם איך שבאמת אתם דבוקים בהשורש אשר שם אין שכחה כלל ואף כל חפצי הגוף מישראל המה ג"כ כבוד שמים
records.targetEnglish: “Recite remembrances before Me”: as it is stated in the Midrash, forgetfulness is found among us. But Israel restrain themselves and set aside all their desires, wishing only for His will. Before making the requests of their prayer they say, “My Lord, open my lips,” indicating that they ask only for what is His will. This is “Recite remembrances before Me so that your remembrance may rise before Me for good”: so that I may show you how you are truly attached to the root, where there is no forgetfulness at all. Even all the bodily desires of Israel are also the honor of Heaven.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim supplies an inner act expressed by “open my lips”: the petitioner relinquishes the demand that prayer serve an independent desire. That surrender makes the mouth a vehicle of divine will. It illuminates why the opening in Rav Tzadok’s paragraph concerns the heart and divine kingship, rather than merely the physical ability to speak. Sod Yesharim develops this within the Rosh Hashanah remembrances; it is not an alternative explanation of the Chanukah law.

records.originHebrew: וְזֶהוּ עִנְיַן קְדֻשַּׁת נֵר חֲנֻכָּה, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי רְאִיַּת הַנֵּרוֹת נִפְעָל בָּזֶה הָאוֹר זָרוּעַ לַצַּדִּיק בְּלֵב נַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ שֶׁמִּצְוַת רְאִיַּת נֵר חֲנֻכָּה פּוֹעֵל לְהֶאָרַת תִּקּוּן הַבְּרִית בַּנֶּפֶשׁ. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (שַׁבָּת כ״ב עַמּוּד א׳): "נֵר שֶׁל חֲנֻכָּה שֶׁהִנִּיחָהּ לְמַעְלָה מֵעֶשְׂרִים אַמָּה פְּסוּלָה", הֲגַם שֶׁהִדְלִיק כַּדִּין בְּכָל דִּקְדּוּקֵי מִצְוָה, וְהַדְלָקָה עוֹשָׂה מִצְוָה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם פְּסוּלָה, מִשּׁוּם דְּלֹא שָׁלְטָה בָּהּ עֵינָא; וְזֶהוּ עִקַּר מִצְוָה שֶׁל נֵר חֲנֻכָּה: "לִרְאוֹתָם בִּלְבָד", וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִקְבָּע הֶאָרָה בַּלֵּב מֵאוֹר זָרוּעַ לַצַּדִּיק.
records.originEnglish: This is the holiness of the Chanukah lamp: seeing the lamps brings about “light sown for the righteous” in the hearts of the souls of Israel. As we have said, the commandment of seeing the Chanukah lamp brings an illumination of the repair of the covenant into the soul. Thus it is written in Shabbat 22a: “A Chanukah lamp placed higher than twenty cubits is invalid.” Even if one kindled it correctly, observing all the details of the commandment—and kindling is what performs the commandment—it is nevertheless invalid because the eye does not take it in. This is the essential point of the Chanukah lamp’s commandment: “only to look at them.” Through this, an illumination from the “light sown for the righteous” becomes established in the heart.
records.themeTitle: The lamp must bring concealed holiness into actual awareness
records.themeSummary: The height limit reveals the purpose of the lamp: a correctly performed act must also make the light perceptible, so that its illumination becomes established within the heart.
records.targetHebrew: וְזֶהוּ הַהֶאָרָה דְּנֵר חֲנֻכָּה שֶׁנִּקְבַּע לְדוֹרוֹת, לְכַלּוֹת עַל יְדֵי אוֹר זֶה כָּל מִינֵי עִרְבּוּבְיָא מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל, הַנִּמְשָׁךְ עַל יְדֵי עִרְבּוּב פְּנִימִיּוּת הַכֹּחוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בִּרְצוֹנוֹת מְעֹרָבוֹת שֶׁאֵינָם מְבֹרָרִים שֶׁהֵם רַק לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם וְלֹא לְשׁוּם מַחֲשָׁבָה וּפְנִיָּה אַחֶרֶת, כָּרָאוּי לְשֹׁרֶשׁ הַיַּהֲדוּת דִּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, אֲשֶׁר הֵם דְּבוּקִים לְגַמְרֵי בֵּאלֹהִים חַיִּים. וּבֶאֱמֶת, כָּל כֹּחַ הַיְסוֹד נִמְשָׁךְ רַק מֵהַנֶּצַח וָהוֹד, וְאִם הַיְסוֹד מְבֹרָר — גַּם נֶצַח וָהוֹד מְבֹרָרִים. אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵצֶל הַיְסוֹד הוּא בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת בַּפֹּעַל, וְאֵצֶל הַנֶּצַח וָהוֹד הוּא עֲדַיִן בַּכֹּחַ, וְהַיְצִיאָה לַפּוֹעַל נֶעְלָם עֲדַיִן. וּמִצַּד הַהֶעְלֵם יֵשׁ מָקוֹם לִטְעוֹת וְצָרִיךְ נֵר לְהָאִיר, וְעַל כֵּן "לְמַעְלָה מֵעֶשְׂרִים פְּסוּלָה, דְּלָא שָׁלְטָא בֵּיהּ עֵינָא", וַעֲדַיִן הוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם. וְעִיקַּר נֵר חֲנֻכָּה לְהוֹצִיא מִן הַהֶעְלֵם לַגִּילּוּי;
records.targetEnglish: This is the illumination of the Chanukah lamp that was established for all generations: by this light, to eliminate every kind of mixture from Israel. Such mixture follows from the inward powers of Israel being mingled with mixed desires, whose being solely for the sake of Heaven—and not for some other thought or ulterior motive—has not been clarified, as befits the root of the Jewish people, the congregation of Israel, who are completely attached to the living God. In truth, all the power of Yesod comes from Netzach and Hod; if Yesod is clarified, Netzach and Hod are also clarified. But in Yesod this is actually manifest, whereas in Netzach and Hod it remains potential: its emergence into actuality is still concealed. Concealment leaves room for error, and a lamp is needed to illuminate. Therefore “above twenty cubits it is invalid, because the eye does not take it in”: it still remains concealed. The essential purpose of the Chanukah lamp is to bring what is concealed into revelation.
records.explanation: Resisei Layla explains exactly why the visible height matters. A potential inner purity can still leave a person vulnerable to mixed motives; the lamp’s task is to bring that hidden condition into recognizable illumination. The same twenty-cubit rule thus expresses the transition that Chanukah 20 calls establishing the light in the heart. The symbolic terms Yesod, Netzach, and Hod are retained with their stated distinction between actuality and potential.

records.targetHebrew: עד עשרים אמה אדם יודע שדר בצל סוכה ולמעלה מעשרים אמה אין אדם יודע וכו' ביאור הענין הוא כדאיתא בגמרא (שם דף ה) למעלה מעשרה מפסקא רשותא והוא כי השי"ת הציב בתפיסת אדם עשר מדות כדכתיב לך ה' הגדולה והגבורה והתפארת וגו' כדי שיהיה להאדם מקום לעבודה באלו המדות וכן יש בהמקור עליון ג"כ עשר דרגין וכפי מה שעובד האדם בעשר שבתפיסתו כך יורד אורו ית' כנגדו מכתרא לכתרא כענין דאיתא בזוה"ק (בא לז) המשפילי לראות דנחית בכתרוי מכתרא לכתרא מנזרא לנזרא מנהירו לנהירו וכו' עד שמתערב תפיסת האדם ביחד עם אורו ית' ואלו שני רשותים כשנתערבו ביחד נקראו עשרים אמה כי מה שנקרא מצד האדם טפח כדכתיב טפחות נתתה ימי נקרא מצד השי"ת אמה וזהו עד עשרים אמה אדם יודע שדר בצל סוכה ולמעלה מעשרים אמה אין אדם יודע שהוא דר בצל סוכה דלא שלטא ביה עינא היינו שאינו כלל בתפיסת אדם כי זה האור העליון שהוא למעלה מעשרים אמה אי אפשר כלל שיתערב ביחד עם תפיסת אדם אולם בתוך עשרים שפיר יכול להתערב ע"י עבודה האור עם תפיסת האדם.
records.targetEnglish: “Up to twenty cubits a person knows that he dwells in the shade of a sukkah; above twenty cubits a person does not know ….” The explanation is as the Gemara says there: “Above ten handbreadths a separate domain begins.” God established ten qualities within human apprehension, as it says, “Yours, Lord, are greatness, might, beauty …,” so that a person would have a place for service within these qualities. In the upper source there are likewise ten levels. Corresponding to a person’s service within the ten that are within human apprehension, His light descends toward the person, from crown to crown, as the Zohar explains “Who lowers Himself to see”: He descends in His crowns, from crown to crown, from diadem to diadem, from light to light, until human apprehension mingles with His light. These two domains, when joined, are called twenty cubits; what is called a handbreadth from the human side—“You have made my days handbreadths”—is called a cubit from God’s side. This is “Up to twenty cubits a person knows that he dwells in the shade of a sukkah; above twenty cubits a person does not know that he dwells in its shade, because the eye does not take it in.” It is entirely outside human apprehension. This upper light, above twenty cubits, cannot mingle with human apprehension at all. Within twenty, however, the light can indeed mingle with human apprehension through service.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim gives the twenty-cubit boundary a precise account of the meeting between divine light and human apprehension. Its subject is the sukkah, but its explanation of “the eye does not take it in” illuminates Rav Tzadok’s insistence that the Chanukah light must actually reach the person: the light must be available to become part of lived awareness. The sukkah’s ten-plus-ten symbolism is presented as its own exposition, not attributed to Rav Tzadok’s lamp teaching.
records.translationProvenance: New English translations of the selected canonical Hebrew, prepared after reading the complete origin section and target paragraph. Clarified antecedents are integrated into the English. The explanation is an editorial comparison, not part of either source.

records.originHebrew: וְאָמְנָם נִצְרָךְ לָזֶה זְכוּת שֶׁיִּזְכֶּה לִרְאוֹת הָאוֹר "כִּי טוֹב", וְהוּא כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹסֵף (סוֹטָה ל״ו עַמּוּד ב׳): "בָּאתָה דְּיוֹקְנוֹ שֶׁל אָבִיו וְנִרְאֲתָה לוֹ וְכוּלֵיהּ", וְהַיְנוּ שֶׁבָּא לוֹ הֶאָרַת אַסְפַּקְלַרְיָא הַמְּאִירָה שֶׁהוּא דְּיוֹקְנוֹ שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב, כִּדְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק א׳ קס״ח עַמּוּד א׳): "מַאן דְּחָמֵי לֵיהּ לְיַעֲקֹב כְּמַאן דְּאִסְתַּכַּל בְּאַסְפַּקְלַרְיָאָה דְּנָהֲרָא", כִּי צוּרָתוֹ שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב חֲקוּקָה בְּכִסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד. וְהִנֵּה אַחַר מַאֲמַר הַגְּמָרָא הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל: "נֵר חֲנֻכָּה שֶׁהִנִּיחָהּ וְכוּלֵיהּ", נִסְמַךְ בַּגְּמָרָא: "דָּרַשׁ רַב נָתָן בַּר מַנְיוֹמֵי מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי תַּנְחוּם: מַאי דִּכְתִיב: 'וְהַבּוֹר רֵק אֵין בּוֹ מָיִם' וְכוּלֵיהּ? מַיִם אֵין בּוֹ, אֲבָל נְחָשִׁים וְעַקְרַבִּים יֵשׁ בּוֹ".
records.originEnglish: Yet merit is required to be privileged to see the light “that it is good.” This is like what is said of Joseph in Sotah 36b: “The image of his father came and appeared to him ….” The illumination of the luminous mirror came to him—Jacob’s image—as the holy Zohar says: “One who sees Jacob is like one who looks into a luminous mirror,” for Jacob’s form is engraved upon the Throne of Glory. Now after the Gemara’s statement just mentioned, “A Chanukah lamp that one placed …,” the Gemara immediately places this teaching: “Rav Natan bar Minyomi expounded in the name of Rabbi Tanchum: What is meant by ‘The pit was empty; there was no water in it …’? There was no water, but there were snakes and scorpions.”
records.themeTitle: Jacob’s image reveals the truth within a confusing desire
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok compares seeing the good Chanukah light to Joseph’s encounter with Jacob’s luminous image. The adjacent teaching about the pit introduces the trials that this illumination must confront.
records.targetHebrew: וּלְמַאן דְּאָמַר: ״לַעֲשׂוֹת צְרָכָיו נִכְנַס״ (סוֹטָה ל״ו עַמּוּד ב׳), נִרְאֶה: דְּיוֹסֵף טָעָה בָּזֶה כִּי יָדַע מַה שֶּׁנִּמְכַּר לְמִצְרַיִם וּלְאוֹתוֹ בַּיִת, וַדַּאי צָרִיךְ לְהוֹצִיא מִשָּׁם נִיצוֹץ קָדוֹשׁ וּרְכוּשׁ גָּדוֹל וְחָשַׁב גַּם כֵּן: אוּלַי הוּא מִמֶּנָּה, וְדִמָּה שֶׁחֶשְׁקוֹ בִּקְדוּשָׁה. וְנִגְלָה לוֹ דְּמוּת דְּיוֹקְנוֹ שֶׁל אָבִיו (סוֹטָה שָׁם) — הַיְינוּ מִדַּת ״אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב״ (מִיכָה ז:כ) וְרָאָה הָאֱמֶת: שֶׁהוּא הֲסָתַת הַיֵּצֶר וְלֹא מִצַּד הַקְּדוּשָׁה כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת הַיּוֹלָד מִמֶּנָּה אֵינוֹ בְּנוֹ כְּלָל, וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהוֹצִיא נִיצוֹץ קָדוֹשׁ עַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה כְּלָל.
records.targetEnglish: According to the opinion that “he entered to attend to his needs,” it seems that Joseph made a mistake in this matter. He knew that his having been sold into Egypt and into that household must mean that he needed to bring a holy spark and great wealth out of there. He also thought: perhaps it is from her; he imagined that his desire was holy. The image of his father was revealed to him—namely, the quality of “truth to Jacob”—and he saw the truth: this was the enticement of the inclination, not something proceeding from holiness. For in truth, a child born to him from her would not be his son at all, and it is impossible to extract a holy spark by this route.
records.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim explains the moral clarity carried by the luminous image. Joseph could mistakenly construe desire as a mission to recover holiness; Jacob’s quality of truth exposes that mistaken construction. This makes the image in Chanukah 20 an illumination that distinguishes genuine holiness from a persuasive religious justification. The passage explicitly presents its reading according to one Talmudic opinion; that qualification remains in the translation.

records.originHebrew: וְכַאֲשֶׁר הֻשְׁלַךְ לַבּוֹר נְחָשִׁים וְעַקְרַבִּים וְלֹא הֲרָגָם, אָז יָדַע יוֹסֵף שֶׁנִּזְדַּמְּנוּ לְהָרְגוֹ וְנַעֲשָׂה לוֹ נֵס, וְאָז הִרְגִּישׁ בְּנַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁנִּצְרָךְ לוֹ לְהִתְבָּרֵר בִּשְׁנֵי הַדְּבָרִים: שֶׁהוֹצִיא דִּבָּה עַל אֶחָיו שֶׁתּוֹלִים עֵינֵיהֶם בִּבְנוֹת הָאָרֶץ, וְשֶׁחֲשׁוּדִים עַל אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי, כִּי לְעִנְיָן זֶה נִזְדַּמְּנוּ לוֹ הַנְּחָשִׁים וְעַקְרַבִּים: כִּי הַנָּחָשׁ שֹׁרֶשׁ שֶׁל פְּגַם הַבְּרִית, שֶׁהוּא עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ שֶׁהִכְנִיס לְאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן בְּתַאֲוַת הָאֲכִילָה, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה נֶעֱנַשׁ בְּ"נָחָשׁ עָפָר לַחְמוֹ", שֶׁנִּטַּל מִמֶּנּוּ הַטַּעַם שֶׁל תַּאֲוַת אֲכִילָה; וְהָעַקְרָב הוּא הַמֵּמִית בְּוַדַּאי, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בְּרָכוֹת ל״ג עַמּוּד א׳): "אֲבָל עַקְרָב פּוֹסֵק", וְהוּא נֶגֶד פְּגַם רְצִיחָה שֶׁנִּמְשַׁךְ עַל יְדֵי קַיִן, וְהוּא נֶגֶד פְּגַם שֶׁל אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי, שֶׁנִּזְהָרִים בָּזֶה גַּם אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם מִצַּד שֶׁהוּא אַכְזָרִיּוּת גְּדוֹלָה, חוּץ הָאִסּוּר שֶׁנֶּאֱסַר לִבְנֵי נֹחַ, וְלָכֵן נִתְבַּיֵּשׁ נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר כְּשֶׁאָכַל אַרְנֶבֶת חַיָּה (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב נְדָרִים ס״ה עַמּוּד א׳). וְכַאֲשֶׁר נִזְדַּמְּנוּ לִפְנֵי יוֹסֵף הַנְּחָשִׁים וְעַקְרַבִּים, הִרְגִּישׁ בְּנַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְהִתְבָּרֵר בְּעִנְיַן הוֹצָאַת הַדִּבָּה, וּבְוַדַּאי עָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה עַל שְׁנֵי הַפְּגָמִים הַנִּזְכָּרִים לְעֵיל.
records.originEnglish: When Joseph was thrown into the pit of snakes and scorpions and did not kill them, he knew that they had been sent to kill him and that a miracle had been performed for him. He then sensed within himself that he needed clarification concerning two matters: his accusation that his brothers set their eyes on the daughters of the land, and his suspicion that they ate a limb from a living animal. The snakes and scorpions had been sent to him for this purpose. The snake is the root of the blemish of the covenant: the serpent’s instigation that introduced desire for eating into Adam. It was therefore punished with “dust is the serpent’s bread,” deprived of the taste of the desire for food. The scorpion certainly kills, as Berakhot 33a states, “For a scorpion, however, one interrupts prayer.” It corresponds to the blemish of murder that extended through Cain, and to the blemish of a limb from a living animal. Even the nations take care about this because of its great cruelty, apart from the prohibition placed upon the descendants of Noah; this is why Nebuchadnezzar was ashamed when he ate a living hare, as stated in Nedarim 65a. When the snakes and scorpions appeared before Joseph, he sensed that he needed clarification concerning his slander, and he certainly repented for the two blemishes mentioned above.
records.themeTitle: A frightening rescue can call a person to examine an earlier judgment
records.themeSummary: Joseph reads the dangers in the pit as a summons to examine the accusations he brought against his brothers. The rescue does not certify that his earlier judgment was complete or faultless.
records.targetHebrew: כְּשֶׁאָדָם מִתְיַסֵּר בְּאֵיזֶה אֵבֶר אוֹ בְּאֵיזֶה כֹּחַ מִכֹּחוֹתָיו כִּי ע' כֹּחוֹת בַּנֶּפֶשׁ נֶגֶד ע' אֻמּוֹת בָּרָע כַּיָּדוּעַ], מִסְּתָמָא בּוֹ חָטָא, וּמִיָּד שֶׁלָּקָה, הֲרֵי הוּא כְּאָחִיךָ, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מַכּוֹת כג.) וַאֲפִילּוּ רַק כְּפָתוּהוּ וְכוּלֵי כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמַכּוֹת (שָׁם), וְכִדְבָרֵי שַׁמַּאי בְּשַׁבָּת (קכא:) בְּנָחָשׁ שֶׁהָיָה רוֹדֵף אַחֲרָיו, כִּי בָּזֶה יָצָא יְדֵי עוֹנְשׁוֹ וְיִסּוּרִין שֶׁלּוֹ בַּפַּחַד שֶׁחָשַׁב שֶׁיִּשְּׁכֶנּוּ; וְכֵן הָיָה בֶּאֱמֶת דְּמִן הַשָּׁמַיִם נִזְדַּמְּנוּ וְכוּלֵי כִּדְאִיתָא הָתָם, רַק שֶׁחָסוּ עָלָיו וּפְדָאוּהוּ עַל יְדֵי הַפַּחַד, עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת נה.): חֶלְמָא בִּישָׁא וְכוּלֵי, כִּי כְּשֶׁשָּׁב בֶּאֱמֶת, אָז כָּל עִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא כְּחוֹלְמִים; וְאָז אוֹתוֹ אֵבֶר וְכֹחַ מְתוּקָּן, וְנֶפֶשׁ מֵשִׁיב אֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ, שֶׁאוֹתוֹ אֵבֶר יֵשׁ בּוֹ תִּיקּוּן, אֶלָּא שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְהוֹסִיף וּלְחַזְּקוֹ. וְאָז "בִּמְקוֹם אֲשֶׁר יֵאָמֵר לָהֶם לֹא עַמִּי אַתֶּם יֵאָמֵר לָהֶם בְּנֵי אֵל חָי]" (הוֹשֵׁעַ ב, א) – דַּיְיקָא בְּאוֹתוֹ מָקוֹם הוּא מַמָּשׁ לְהֵיפֶךְ:
records.targetEnglish: When a person suffers in a particular limb or one of the soul’s powers—for there are seventy powers in the soul corresponding to the seventy nations on the side of evil, as is known—it is presumable that the sin was in that place. As soon as he has been punished, he is again “your brother,” as our Sages say in Makkot 23a. This applies even if they only bound him, as stated there. Likewise, as stated in Shabbat 121b about a snake pursuing a person: he has discharged his punishment and suffering through the fear that it would bite him. Indeed, it really had been sent from Heaven, as stated there; but they had compassion on him and redeemed him through the fear. This is like what is said in Berakhot 55a about a bad dream: for when one truly repents, all the matters of this world are like dreams. Then that limb and power are repaired, and “the soul restores the soul”: that limb has a repair, but one must add to it and strengthen it. Then, “In the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ it will be said to them, ‘Children of the living God’”—in precisely that place, the matter becomes its very opposite.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik reads the same encounter with a snake as more than either injury or escape: the fear itself can accomplish a stage of repair when joined to real repentance. It also insists that the repaired power still needs strengthening. That gives a concrete account of why Joseph can be saved and yet take the event as a demand for inward work. This is the author’s spiritual interpretation, not a license to identify another person’s suffering with a particular fault.
records.translationProvenance: New English translations after full-context review. The canonical Hebrew’s expansion כדברי שמאי at the Shabbat citation is retained unchanged, but the primary Sefaria witness, Tzidkat HaTzadick, Lublin, 1913, reads וכד״ש rather than naming Shammai (https://www.sefaria.org/api/texts/Tzidkat_HaTzadik.161?context=0, inspected 2026-10-20). The English therefore says “as stated in Shabbat 121b.” Canonical section-heading debris after the argument is outside the selected quotation.

records.originHebrew: וְכַאֲשֶׁר הֻשְׁלַךְ לַבּוֹר נְחָשִׁים וְעַקְרַבִּים וְלֹא הֲרָגָם, אָז יָדַע יוֹסֵף שֶׁנִּזְדַּמְּנוּ לְהָרְגוֹ וְנַעֲשָׂה לוֹ נֵס, וְאָז הִרְגִּישׁ בְּנַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁנִּצְרָךְ לוֹ לְהִתְבָּרֵר בִּשְׁנֵי הַדְּבָרִים: שֶׁהוֹצִיא דִּבָּה עַל אֶחָיו שֶׁתּוֹלִים עֵינֵיהֶם בִּבְנוֹת הָאָרֶץ, וְשֶׁחֲשׁוּדִים עַל אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי, כִּי לְעִנְיָן זֶה נִזְדַּמְּנוּ לוֹ הַנְּחָשִׁים וְעַקְרַבִּים: כִּי הַנָּחָשׁ שֹׁרֶשׁ שֶׁל פְּגַם הַבְּרִית, שֶׁהוּא עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ שֶׁהִכְנִיס לְאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן בְּתַאֲוַת הָאֲכִילָה, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה נֶעֱנַשׁ בְּ"נָחָשׁ עָפָר לַחְמוֹ", שֶׁנִּטַּל מִמֶּנּוּ הַטַּעַם שֶׁל תַּאֲוַת אֲכִילָה; וְהָעַקְרָב הוּא הַמֵּמִית בְּוַדַּאי, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בְּרָכוֹת ל״ג עַמּוּד א׳): "אֲבָל עַקְרָב פּוֹסֵק", וְהוּא נֶגֶד פְּגַם רְצִיחָה שֶׁנִּמְשַׁךְ עַל יְדֵי קַיִן, וְהוּא נֶגֶד פְּגַם שֶׁל אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי, שֶׁנִּזְהָרִים בָּזֶה גַּם אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם מִצַּד שֶׁהוּא אַכְזָרִיּוּת גְּדוֹלָה, חוּץ הָאִסּוּר שֶׁנֶּאֱסַר לִבְנֵי נֹחַ, וְלָכֵן נִתְבַּיֵּשׁ נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר כְּשֶׁאָכַל אַרְנֶבֶת חַיָּה (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב נְדָרִים ס״ה עַמּוּד א׳). וְכַאֲשֶׁר נִזְדַּמְּנוּ לִפְנֵי יוֹסֵף הַנְּחָשִׁים וְעַקְרַבִּים, הִרְגִּישׁ בְּנַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְהִתְבָּרֵר בְּעִנְיַן הוֹצָאַת הַדִּבָּה, וּבְוַדַּאי עָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה עַל שְׁנֵי הַפְּגָמִים הַנִּזְכָּרִים לְעֵיל.
records.originEnglish: When Joseph was thrown into the pit of snakes and scorpions and did not kill them, he knew that they had been sent to kill him and that a miracle had been performed for him. He then sensed within himself that he needed clarification concerning two matters: his accusation that his brothers set their eyes on the daughters of the land, and his suspicion that they ate a limb from a living animal. The snakes and scorpions had been sent to him for this purpose. The snake is the root of the blemish of the covenant: the serpent’s instigation that introduced desire for eating into Adam. It was therefore punished with “dust is the serpent’s bread,” deprived of the taste of the desire for food. The scorpion certainly kills, as Berakhot 33a states, “For a scorpion, however, one interrupts prayer.” It corresponds to the blemish of murder that extended through Cain, and to the blemish of a limb from a living animal. Even the nations take care about this because of its great cruelty, apart from the prohibition placed upon the descendants of Noah; this is why Nebuchadnezzar was ashamed when he ate a living hare, as stated in Nedarim 65a. When the snakes and scorpions appeared before Joseph, he sensed that he needed clarification concerning his slander, and he certainly repented for the two blemishes mentioned above.
records.themeTitle: A frightening rescue can call a person to examine an earlier judgment
records.themeSummary: Joseph reads the dangers in the pit as a summons to examine the accusations he brought against his brothers. The rescue does not certify that his earlier judgment was complete or faultless.
records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayeshev 4
records.targetHebrew: וְהוּא כְּשֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חָפֵץ לְנַסּוֹת אֶת הָאָדָם אָז מְשַׁכֵּחַ מִמֶּנּוּ כָּל חוֹמֶר הָאִיסּוּר מֵהַדָּבָר שֶׁרוֹצֶה לְנַסּוֹתוֹ בּוֹ, וְזֶה גַּם כֵּן הָיָה עִנְיַן הַשְּׁבָטִים כַּאֲשֶׁר רָצוּ לְהָרְגוֹ אָז נֶעְלַם מֵהֶם כָּל הָאִיסּוּר וְרַק בְּעֵצוֹת זוּלַת דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה נִיצַּל מִיָּדָם וְגַם הֵם נִיצּוֹלוּ מֵעָוֹן, כִּי יְהוּדָא הָיָה חָכָם גָּדוֹל בְּחָכְמוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה עַל כֵּן זָמַם עֵצָה וְאָמַר "מַה בֶּצַע" פֵּירוּשׁ אַף שֶׁהָיָה נִרְאֶה לוֹ שֶׁמִּצַּד הַדִּין מוּתָּר לְהָרְגוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁיִּתְבָּאֵר אַךְ מָה הֲנָאָה יַגִּיעַ לָנוּ מִזֶּה. [וְכִי יִתֵּן לִי אָבִי הַכְּתוֹנֶת פַּסִּים, הֲלֹא עִנְיַן הַכְּתוֹנֶת פַּסִּים שַׁיָּיךְ רַק לְיוֹסֵף. תַּשְׁלוּם.] [ ] וְכִי בִּשְׁבִיל זֶה יֹאהֲבֶנּוּ אָבִינוּ בְּיוֹתֵר, וּמִיָּד כְּשֶׁהוּסְכַּם בֵּינֵיהֶם שֶׁלֹּא יַהַרְגוּ אוֹתוֹ רָאוּ חוֹמֶר הָאִיסּוּר שֶׁאָסוּר לְהָרְגוֹ מִצַּד הַדִּין גַּם כֵּן, וְזֹאת הָעֵצָה שֶׁעַל פִּי חָכְמַת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה אָסוּר לְאָדָם שֶׁיָּגֵן עִמָּהּ בַּעֲדוֹ בְּכָל עֵת רַק בְּעֵת הַנִּסָּיוֹן שֶׁאֵין עֵצָה אַחֶרֶת, אֲבָל לִפְרוֹשׁ מֵאִיסּוּר בָּעֵת שֶׁזּוֹכֵר שֶׁהַדָּבָר אָסוּר, אָסוּר לוֹ לִפְרוֹשׁ אֶת עַצְמוֹ עַל פִּי עֵצָה כָּזֹאת רַק מֵחֲמַת פְּקוּדָּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ. וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ הַגְּמָרָא כָּל הַמְבָרֵךְ אֶת יְהוּדָא הַיְינוּ שֶׁיָּשָׁר הַדָּבָר בְּעֵינָיו לַעֲשׂוֹת תָּמִיד כֵּן נִקְרָא בּוֹצֵעַ כִּי יְהוּדָא גַּם כֵּן לֹא לָקַח לוֹ עֵצָה הַזֹּאת בִּלְתִּי בִּשְׁעַת הַנִּסָּיוֹן.
records.targetEnglish: When God wishes to test a person, He causes the person to forget the full severity of the prohibition concerning the matter in which He wishes to test him. This was also the matter of the tribes, Joseph’s brothers. When they wished to kill him, the whole prohibition was concealed from them. Only through counsel other than words of Torah was he saved from their hands, and they too were saved from sin. Judah was very wise in worldly matters; he therefore devised advice and said, “What profit?” Even though it appeared to him that killing him was legally permitted, as will be explained, what benefit would come to us from it? (Would my father give me the striped coat? The striped coat belongs specifically to Joseph. Supplement.) Would our father love us more because of this? As soon as they agreed not to kill him, they saw the gravity of the prohibition: killing him was also legally forbidden. A person may not use this advice based on worldly wisdom as his protection at all times, but only at the time of a test when no other counsel is available. When one remembers that something is prohibited, it is forbidden to withdraw from it on the basis of such advice; one must withdraw because of His command. This explains the Gemara: “Anyone who blesses Judah”—meaning that he approves of acting this way always—“is called one who compromises.” Judah, too, used this advice only at the time of the test.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach examines the brothers’ side of the same danger: in the test, a lethal judgment could appear legally justified until a different counsel interrupted it. This deepens the section’s warning that an apparently sound judgment about a brother can require subsequent clarification. Its exceptional use of worldly advice is carefully limited to a test in which Torah’s prohibition has become concealed; the author forbids substituting self-interest for obedience when the prohibition is remembered.
records.translationProvenance: New English translations after reading the complete origin section and target paragraph. The target’s striped-coat supplement is retained and translated in parentheses as a marked supplement; an empty inherited bracket pair has no English content. “Joseph’s brothers” identifies the antecedent. The explanation does not treat the exceptional counsel as ordinary permission.

records.originHebrew: וְאַחַר כָּל זֶה, כְּשֶׁנִּמְכַּר לְעֶבֶד, נִתְוַדַּע לוֹ שֶׁנִּצְרָךְ עוֹד בֵּרוּרִים בָּזֶה, שֶׁלֹּא נִתְקַן עוֹד בִּשְׁלֵמוּת הַפְּגָם; וְגַם אַחַר זֶה שֶׁנִּזְדַּמֵּן לוֹ הַנִּסָּיוֹן וְזָכָה לְהָאוֹר זָרוּעַ לַצַּדִּיק שֶׁנִּרְאָה לוֹ דְּמוּת דְּיוֹקְנוֹ שֶׁל אָבִיו כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל וְעָמַד בַּנִּסָּיוֹן, הוּצְרַךְ עוֹד לְבֵרוּרִים, "עִנּוּ בַכֶּבֶל רַגְלוֹ", "עַד עֵת בֹּא דְבָרוֹ, אִמְרַת הַשֵּׁם צְרָפָתְהוּ". וּמִזֶּה יָדִין כָּל אָדָם בְּנַפְשׁוֹ: שֶׁגַּם אִם זָכָה לִפְעָמִים לְהָאִיר בְּנַפְשׁוֹ מִבְּחִינַת הָאוֹר זָרוּעַ לַצַּדִּיק, בַּל יֹאמַר בְּלִבּוֹ: "שָׁלוֹם עָלַיִךְ נַפְשִׁי, וּכְבָר זִכִּיתִי לִבִּי", כִּי בְּוַדַּאי עוֹד נִצְרָךְ בָּזֶה לְבֵרוּרִים בְּכָל יָמָיו, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (סֻכָּה נ״ב עַמּוּד ב׳): "יִצְרוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם מִתְגַּבֵּר עָלָיו בְּכָל יוֹם, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: 'צוֹפֶה רָשָׁע לַצַּדִּיק'", "לַצַּדִּיק" דַּוְקָא הַיְנוּ מִי שֶׁגּוֹדֵר עַצְמוֹ לְתַקֵּן הַפְּגָם, וְעִם כָּל זֶה נִצְרָךְ לְבֵרוּרִים בְּכָל יוֹם, וְ"אִלְמָלֵא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שֶׁעוֹזְרוֹ אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לוֹ".
records.originEnglish: Even after all this, when Joseph was sold as a slave he learned that further clarifications were needed: the blemish had not yet been completely repaired. Later, too, when the test came to him, he merited the “light sown for the righteous,” his father’s image appeared to him as mentioned above, and he withstood the test, he still required further clarifications: “They afflicted his feet with fetters,” “until the time his word came; the word of the Lord refined him.” Every person should judge himself by this. Even if one has sometimes merited illumination within the soul from the “light sown for the righteous,” one must not say in one’s heart, “Peace be upon you, my soul; I have already purified my heart.” Certainly, further clarifications are needed throughout one’s life. As Sukkah 52b says, “A person’s inclination grows stronger against him every day, as it says, ‘The wicked watches for the righteous.’” It says specifically “the righteous”—one who fences himself in to repair the blemish. Even so, clarification is needed every day, and “were it not for the Holy One, blessed be He, helping him, he could not overcome it.”
records.themeTitle: A genuine victory does not finish the work of clarification
records.themeSummary: Joseph’s rescue and resistance are real achievements, yet further trials follow. Rav Tzadok turns that sequence into a lifelong requirement for renewed scrutiny and divine help.
records.targetHebrew: אמנם דבר שפתים שלו היה אך למחסור ע"י שאמר לשר המשקים זכרתני והזכרתני. וזה לא נחשב בעיניו לשום חטא כי באמת לא בטח בשר המשקים כמ"ש אשר שם ה' מבטחו זה יוסף רק לאשר הרגיש שבאמת סיבת תשועתו יהיה ע"י שר המשקים רצה שיהיה נעשה הישועה ע"פ הטבע כי אין סומכין על הנם. ועכ"ז היה לו למחסור שע"י זה נתוסף לו ב' שנים לעוררו בזה על הדבר שפתים שהביא דבה על אחיו שהיה נדמה לו ג"כ שהוא דבר קל. ובאמת נסתעף מזה שני הפגמים הנ"ל כי לה"ר והוצאת דבה בא מסבת קנאה וכעס וברית הלשון מכוון נגד ברית המעור כידוע. ודבר שפתים כאלו המה מעונות שאדם דש בעקביו והם אך למחסור ועי"ז נתוסף לו ב' שנים לעוררו שנצרך לתקן פגם השני ימים ע"י הדבר שפתים. וע"ז מרמז ויהי מקץ שנתים ימים היינו כאשר נתקנו פגם השני ימים כנ"ל ופרעה חולם וכמש"נ עד עת בא דברו אמרת ה' צרפתהו:
records.targetEnglish: But Joseph’s words were “only a loss,” through his saying to the chief cupbearer, “Remember me” and “mention me.” He did not regard this as any sin, for he really did not put his trust in the chief cupbearer—as it says, “Who places his trust in the Lord”: this is Joseph. Rather, because he sensed that the cause of his deliverance would in fact be the chief cupbearer, he wanted the deliverance to come about through nature, since one does not rely on a miracle. Nevertheless, it was a loss to him: two years were added, to awaken him regarding the words with which he had slandered his brothers, which had likewise seemed a slight matter to him. In truth, the two blemishes mentioned above branched out from this, for malicious speech and slander come from jealousy and anger, and the covenant of the tongue corresponds to the covenant of the sexual organ, as is known. Such words are among the sins a person treads underfoot, and they bring only loss. Through this, two years were added to awaken him to the need to repair the blemish of the two days through the correction of his words. This is hinted at by “At the end of two years of days”: when the blemish of the two days was repaired, “Pharaoh dreamed,” as it says, “Until the time his word came; the word of the Lord refined him.”
records.explanation: Miketz identifies a specific reason why Joseph’s successful resistance did not end his refining: he could still overlook the force of his own speech. The passage expressly preserves Joseph’s trust in God; the extra years expose a subtler flaw rather than proving that the earlier faith and victory were false. Its “two days” refers, in the complete paragraph, to the distorted forms of kindness and strength that produce desire and anger.
records.translationProvenance: New English translations after full origin-section and full target-paragraph review. The English identifies Joseph and the implied correction of his speech. The target’s “two days” retains its own symbolic formulation; the explanation identifies the kindness/strength and desire/anger antecedents established earlier in the full paragraph.

records.originHebrew: וְאַחַר כָּל זֶה, כְּשֶׁנִּמְכַּר לְעֶבֶד, נִתְוַדַּע לוֹ שֶׁנִּצְרָךְ עוֹד בֵּרוּרִים בָּזֶה, שֶׁלֹּא נִתְקַן עוֹד בִּשְׁלֵמוּת הַפְּגָם; וְגַם אַחַר זֶה שֶׁנִּזְדַּמֵּן לוֹ הַנִּסָּיוֹן וְזָכָה לְהָאוֹר זָרוּעַ לַצַּדִּיק שֶׁנִּרְאָה לוֹ דְּמוּת דְּיוֹקְנוֹ שֶׁל אָבִיו כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל וְעָמַד בַּנִּסָּיוֹן, הוּצְרַךְ עוֹד לְבֵרוּרִים, "עִנּוּ בַכֶּבֶל רַגְלוֹ", "עַד עֵת בֹּא דְבָרוֹ, אִמְרַת הַשֵּׁם צְרָפָתְהוּ". וּמִזֶּה יָדִין כָּל אָדָם בְּנַפְשׁוֹ: שֶׁגַּם אִם זָכָה לִפְעָמִים לְהָאִיר בְּנַפְשׁוֹ מִבְּחִינַת הָאוֹר זָרוּעַ לַצַּדִּיק, בַּל יֹאמַר בְּלִבּוֹ: "שָׁלוֹם עָלַיִךְ נַפְשִׁי, וּכְבָר זִכִּיתִי לִבִּי", כִּי בְּוַדַּאי עוֹד נִצְרָךְ בָּזֶה לְבֵרוּרִים בְּכָל יָמָיו, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (סֻכָּה נ״ב עַמּוּד ב׳): "יִצְרוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם מִתְגַּבֵּר עָלָיו בְּכָל יוֹם, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: 'צוֹפֶה רָשָׁע לַצַּדִּיק'", "לַצַּדִּיק" דַּוְקָא הַיְנוּ מִי שֶׁגּוֹדֵר עַצְמוֹ לְתַקֵּן הַפְּגָם, וְעִם כָּל זֶה נִצְרָךְ לְבֵרוּרִים בְּכָל יוֹם, וְ"אִלְמָלֵא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שֶׁעוֹזְרוֹ אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לוֹ".
records.originEnglish: Even after all this, when Joseph was sold as a slave he learned that further clarifications were needed: the blemish had not yet been completely repaired. Later, too, when the test came to him, he merited the “light sown for the righteous,” his father’s image appeared to him as mentioned above, and he withstood the test, he still required further clarifications: “They afflicted his feet with fetters,” “until the time his word came; the word of the Lord refined him.” Every person should judge himself by this. Even if one has sometimes merited illumination within the soul from the “light sown for the righteous,” one must not say in one’s heart, “Peace be upon you, my soul; I have already purified my heart.” Certainly, further clarifications are needed throughout one’s life. As Sukkah 52b says, “A person’s inclination grows stronger against him every day, as it says, ‘The wicked watches for the righteous.’” It says specifically “the righteous”—one who fences himself in to repair the blemish. Even so, clarification is needed every day, and “were it not for the Holy One, blessed be He, helping him, he could not overcome it.”
records.themeTitle: A genuine victory does not finish the work of clarification
records.themeSummary: Joseph’s rescue and resistance are real achievements, yet further trials follow. Rav Tzadok turns that sequence into a lifelong requirement for renewed scrutiny and divine help.
records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 1
records.targetHebrew: וַיְהִי מִקֵּץ שְׁנָתַיִם יָמִים. בַּזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית קוּף צָדִי גִּימֶל עַמּוּד בֵּית) רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר פָּתַח "חַי הַשֵּׁם וּבָרוּךְ צוּרִי וְיָרוּם אֱלֹקֵי יִשְׁעִי". "חַי הַשֵּׁם" הַיְינוּ מִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ לֵב טָהוֹר וּמְנוּקֶּה מִכָּל חֶמְדּוֹת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם רַק דָּבוּק בְּחַיִּים נִצְחִיִּים, "וּבָרוּךְ צוּרִי" הַיְינוּ מִי שֶׁמַּכִּיר שֶׁכָּל הַטּוֹבוֹת הֵם רַק מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְלָכֵן יֵשׁ לוֹ עַיִן טוֹבָה, אָז "וְיָרוּם אֱלֹקֵי יִשְׁעִי" הַיְינוּ שֶׁיַּשִּׂיג יְשׁוּעוֹת גְּבוֹהִים, יוֹתֵר מִכְּפִי שִׂכְלוֹ. כִּי טֶרֶם יִתְבָּרֵר הָאָדָם בְּאֵלּוּ דְּבָרִים הַנִּזְכָּרִים אֵין בְּאֶפְשָׁר לִתֵּן לוֹ יְשׁוּעוֹת כִּי עוֹד אֵינוֹ כְּלִי בָּהִיר לְקַבֵּל, וְלָזֹאת "וַיְהִי מִקֵּץ שְׁנָתַיִם יָמִים" הַיְינוּ אַחַר שֶׁנִּתְבָּרֵר בְּאֵלּוּ הַשְּׁנֵי דְּבָרִים, אָז חָלַם פַּרְעֹה וְהִשִּׂיג תֵּיכֶף יְשׁוּעָה, "עַד עֵת בֹּא דְבָרוֹ אִמְרַת הַשֵּׁם צְרָפָתְהוּ", כִּי בַּלַּיְלָה הַהוּא גָּדְלָה צַעֲקַת יוֹסֵף הַצַּדִּיק "שׁוּבָה הַשֵּׁם עַד מָתָי" וְתֵיכֶף הִשִּׂיג יְשׁוּעָה. וְעַל זֶה כְּתִיב (תְּהִלִּים פֵּא חֵית, בֵּית) "הַשֵּׁם אֱלֹקֵי יְשׁוּעָתִי וְכוּלֵי צָעַקְתִּי בַלַּיְלָה נֶגְדֶּךָ", כִּי כָּךְ הוּא מִדּוֹתָיו שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא טֶרֶם אֲשֶׁר יִתֵּן הַיְשׁוּעָה מֵבִיא בְּלֵב הָאָדָם צְעָקָה בָּזֶה לְמַעַן אֲשֶׁר יִקָּרֵא "יְגִיעַ כַּפֶּיךָ".
records.targetEnglish: “At the end of two years of days.” In the holy Zohar, Rabbi Elazar opens with “The Lord lives; blessed is my rock; exalted be the God of my salvation.” “The Lord lives” means one whose heart is pure and cleansed of all the world’s desires, attached only to eternal life. “Blessed is my rock” means one who recognizes that all good things come only from God, and therefore has a generous eye. Then, “Exalted be the God of my salvation”: he will attain deliverances higher than his understanding. Before a person is clarified in these matters, it is impossible to give him deliverances, for he is not yet a clear vessel to receive them. Therefore, “At the end of two years of days” means after he was clarified in these two matters. Then Pharaoh dreamed, and he immediately attained deliverance: “Until the time his word came; the word of the Lord refined him.” That night Joseph the righteous cried out greatly, “Return, Lord—how long?” and immediately attained deliverance. Of this it is written, “Lord, God of my salvation … I have cried out at night before You.” For this is the Holy One’s way: before giving deliverance, He places a cry in the person’s heart, so that it may be called “the labor of your hands.”
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explains what the prolonged refinement prepares: a heart freed from grasping desire and a generous recognition that good comes from God. Even the final cry is awakened by God, while becoming the person’s own labor. This illuminates both halves of Rav Tzadok’s conclusion—continued work and the indispensable divine help—without treating deliverance as something a person can demand after one successful test.

records.originHebrew: וְעַל זֶה יִרְמֹז סְמִיכוּת הַמַּאֲמָר "אֲבָל נְחָשִׁים וְעַקְרַבִּים יֵשׁ בּוֹ" לַמַּאֲמָר הָרִאשׁוֹן בְּנֵר חֲנֻכָּה, שֶׁהָעִקָּר בְּמִצְוַת הָרְאִיָּה שֶׁזּוֹכִין עַל יְדֵי זֶה לִבְחִינַת אוֹר זָרוּעַ לַצַּדִּיק לִהְיוֹת נִתְקָן פְּגַם הַבְּרִית כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל; וְנִסְמַךְ זֶה הַמַּאֲמָר כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יִסְמֹךְ הָאָדָם בְּנַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁכְּבָר נִתְקַן הַכֹּל, רַק יֵדַע דִּימֵי חֲנֻכָּה הֵמָּה הֲכָנָה וְחִנּוּךְ מִבְּחִינַת הָאוֹר זָרוּעַ לַצַּדִּיק, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה יִזְכֶּה לִשְׁלֵמוּת הַתִּקּוּן בִּימֵי שׁוֹבָבִי"ם; וְהָעִקָּר לִהְיוֹת נִזְהָר בְּנַפְשׁוֹ מֵהִרְהוּר וּרְאִיָּה, שֶׁעַל זֶה מוֹרֶה שֶׁנִּבְרָא חֹדֶשׁ זֶה בְּאוֹת עַיִ״ן שֶׁהוּא הֲכָנַת הַתִּקּוּן בִּשְׁמִירַת הָעֵינַיִם, וּכְמַה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְלֹא תָתוּרוּ וְגוֹמֵר וְאַחֲרֵי עֵינֵיכֶם", וְאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת י״ב עַמּוּד ב׳): "זֶה הִרְהוּר עֲבֵרָה", כִּי עַל יְדֵי שְׁמִירַת עֵינַיִם נִיצוֹלִים מֵהִרְהוּר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כ״ח עַמּוּד ב׳): "דְּשׁוּרְיָינֵי דְּעֵינָא בְּאוּבַנְתָּא דְּלִבָּא תָּלוּ". וּבְכָל שָׁנָה וְשָׁנָה בִּזְמַנִּים אֵלּוּ נִפְעָל הַתִּקּוּן וְהַבֵּרוּר בְּנַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּעֵזֶר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ; וְכַאֲשֶׁר יִתֵּן הָאָדָם אֶל לִבּוֹ לְתַקֵּן, יָשִׂים הַשֵּׁם מִבְטַחוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נִתְקָן בִּשְׁלֵמוּת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּיוֹסֵף (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה פ״ט): "'אַשְׁרֵי הַגֶּבֶר אֲשֶׁר שָׂם הַשֵּׁם מִבְטַחוֹ' זֶה יוֹסֵף".
records.originEnglish: This is what is hinted at by placing “but there were snakes and scorpions in it” next to the first teaching about the Chanukah lamp. The essential point of the commandment is seeing, through which one merits the quality of “light sown for the righteous,” repairing the blemish of the covenant as mentioned above. This statement follows it so that a person will not rely upon the thought that everything has already been repaired. Rather, one should know that Chanukah is a preparation and initiation into the “light sown for the righteous,” through which one may merit the completeness of the repair during the days of Shovavim. The essential thing is to guard oneself in thought and sight. This is indicated by this month’s being created with the letter ayin: the preparation for repair through guarding the eyes. As it says, “Do not stray … after your eyes,” which Berakhot 12b explains as thoughts of transgression. Guarding the eyes saves one from such thoughts, as Avodah Zarah 28b says, “The vessels of the eye are attached to the chambers of the heart.” Every year, in these seasons, repair and clarification are brought about in the souls of Israel, with God’s help. When a person takes repair to heart, let him place his trust in God that he will be completely repaired, as is said of Joseph in Genesis Rabbah 89: “‘Happy is the man who makes the Lord his trust’—this is Joseph.”
records.themeTitle: Guarding sight must deepen into the repair of the heart
records.themeSummary: Chanukah begins a recurring season of repair rather than certifying its completion. Guarding the eyes prepares the heart, and active attention to repair belongs together with trust in God.
records.targetHebrew: אַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת הָעִיקָּר הַלֵּב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "מִכָּל מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ] כִּי מִמֶּנּוּ תּוֹצְאוֹת חַיִּים" (מִשְׁלֵי ד, כג), שֶׁבּוֹ עִיקַּר הַחַיּוּת וְהַדְּבֵיקוּת בֵּאלֹהִים חַיִּים, וּבָזֶה יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה וְכֻלּוֹ זֶרַע אֱמֶת. וּבִלְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים: "עַיִן יָפָה" וְ"עַיִן טוֹבָה" רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר נְדִיבוּת הַלֵּב וְשֶׁאֵינוֹ מְקַנֵּא, וְכֵן בִּלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב: "טוֹב עַיִן הוּא יְבֹרָךְ] כִּי נָתַן מִלַּחְמוֹ לַדָּל]" (מִשְׁלֵי כב, ט). וְהַהִיפּוּךְ: עַיִן רָעָה, וּבִלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב "רַע עַיִן" (שָׁם כג, ו). וְזֶה הַחִסָּרוֹן הוּא בְּזַרְעָא דְּיוֹסֵף דַּיְיקָא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אֶפְרַיִם לֹא יְקַנֵּא אֶת יְהוּדָה]" (יְשַׁעְיָה יא, יג), כִּי שׁוֹרֶשׁ יוֹסֵף יְרֵא חֵטְא, שֶׁזֶּהוּ שְׁמִירַת הָעַיִן, וְהוּא אוֹתִיּוֹת רְאִיָּ"ה, כְּטַעַם: מַחֲוֵי לְהוּ יִצְחָק הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעֵינַיְיהוּ (שַׁבָּת פט:), שֶׁזֶּה מִכֹּחַ יִצְחָק וּמִמִּדָּתוֹ. וְהַנְּדִיבוּת הוּא מִמִּדַּת הָאַהֲבָה: "חֶסֶד לְאַבְרָהָם" (מִיכָה ז, כ), שֶׁהוּא מַמָּשׁ הַהֵיפֶךְ, וְאִם כֵּן אַדְּרַבָּה, הֵם עֵינֵיהֶם יָפוֹת וּבַעֲלֵי עַיִן טוֹבָה יוֹתֵר מִמֶּנּוּ:
records.targetEnglish: But in truth the heart is primary, as it is written, “More than all you guard, guard your heart, for from it are the issues of life.” In it lies the principal life and attachment to the living God. In this respect Jacob our father’s bed was complete, and all his offspring were a seed of truth. In the Sages’ language, “a generous eye” and “a good eye” mean generosity of heart and the absence of jealousy; likewise in Scripture, “One with a good eye will be blessed, for he has given of his bread to the poor.” The opposite is an evil eye, called “an evil eye” in Scripture. This deficiency is specifically in Joseph’s descendants, as it says, “Ephraim will not envy Judah.” For Joseph’s root is fear of sin, which is guarding the eye; yirah (fear) has the letters of re’iyah, seeing, like the teaching that Isaac points out the Holy One, blessed be He, before their eyes. This comes from Isaac’s power and quality. Generosity comes from the quality of love, “kindness to Abraham,” which is its very opposite. If so, on the contrary, the brothers’ eyes are more generous, and they possess a better eye than he does.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik prevents “guarding the eyes” from becoming the whole definition of a repaired heart. Joseph’s careful restraint must also meet the brothers’ generosity and freedom from jealousy. This supplies a precise further dimension to Chanukah 20’s warning against declaring the work complete: the eye is linked to the heart not only through desire, but also through the way one looks upon another person.

records.originHebrew: וְעַל זֶה יִרְמֹז סְמִיכוּת הַמַּאֲמָר "אֲבָל נְחָשִׁים וְעַקְרַבִּים יֵשׁ בּוֹ" לַמַּאֲמָר הָרִאשׁוֹן בְּנֵר חֲנֻכָּה, שֶׁהָעִקָּר בְּמִצְוַת הָרְאִיָּה שֶׁזּוֹכִין עַל יְדֵי זֶה לִבְחִינַת אוֹר זָרוּעַ לַצַּדִּיק לִהְיוֹת נִתְקָן פְּגַם הַבְּרִית כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל; וְנִסְמַךְ זֶה הַמַּאֲמָר כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יִסְמֹךְ הָאָדָם בְּנַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁכְּבָר נִתְקַן הַכֹּל, רַק יֵדַע דִּימֵי חֲנֻכָּה הֵמָּה הֲכָנָה וְחִנּוּךְ מִבְּחִינַת הָאוֹר זָרוּעַ לַצַּדִּיק, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה יִזְכֶּה לִשְׁלֵמוּת הַתִּקּוּן בִּימֵי שׁוֹבָבִי"ם; וְהָעִקָּר לִהְיוֹת נִזְהָר בְּנַפְשׁוֹ מֵהִרְהוּר וּרְאִיָּה, שֶׁעַל זֶה מוֹרֶה שֶׁנִּבְרָא חֹדֶשׁ זֶה בְּאוֹת עַיִ״ן שֶׁהוּא הֲכָנַת הַתִּקּוּן בִּשְׁמִירַת הָעֵינַיִם, וּכְמַה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְלֹא תָתוּרוּ וְגוֹמֵר וְאַחֲרֵי עֵינֵיכֶם", וְאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת י״ב עַמּוּד ב׳): "זֶה הִרְהוּר עֲבֵרָה", כִּי עַל יְדֵי שְׁמִירַת עֵינַיִם נִיצוֹלִים מֵהִרְהוּר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כ״ח עַמּוּד ב׳): "דְּשׁוּרְיָינֵי דְּעֵינָא בְּאוּבַנְתָּא דְּלִבָּא תָּלוּ". וּבְכָל שָׁנָה וְשָׁנָה בִּזְמַנִּים אֵלּוּ נִפְעָל הַתִּקּוּן וְהַבֵּרוּר בְּנַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּעֵזֶר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ; וְכַאֲשֶׁר יִתֵּן הָאָדָם אֶל לִבּוֹ לְתַקֵּן, יָשִׂים הַשֵּׁם מִבְטַחוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נִתְקָן בִּשְׁלֵמוּת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּיוֹסֵף (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה פ״ט): "'אַשְׁרֵי הַגֶּבֶר אֲשֶׁר שָׂם הַשֵּׁם מִבְטַחוֹ' זֶה יוֹסֵף".
records.originEnglish: This is what is hinted at by placing “but there were snakes and scorpions in it” next to the first teaching about the Chanukah lamp. The essential point of the commandment is seeing, through which one merits the quality of “light sown for the righteous,” repairing the blemish of the covenant as mentioned above. This statement follows it so that a person will not rely upon the thought that everything has already been repaired. Rather, one should know that Chanukah is a preparation and initiation into the “light sown for the righteous,” through which one may merit the completeness of the repair during the days of Shovavim. The essential thing is to guard oneself in thought and sight. This is indicated by this month’s being created with the letter ayin: the preparation for repair through guarding the eyes. As it says, “Do not stray … after your eyes,” which Berakhot 12b explains as thoughts of transgression. Guarding the eyes saves one from such thoughts, as Avodah Zarah 28b says, “The vessels of the eye are attached to the chambers of the heart.” Every year, in these seasons, repair and clarification are brought about in the souls of Israel, with God’s help. When a person takes repair to heart, let him place his trust in God that he will be completely repaired, as is said of Joseph in Genesis Rabbah 89: “‘Happy is the man who makes the Lord his trust’—this is Joseph.”
records.themeTitle: Guarding sight must deepen into the repair of the heart
records.themeSummary: Chanukah begins a recurring season of repair rather than certifying its completion. Guarding the eyes prepares the heart, and active attention to repair belongs together with trust in God.
records.targetHebrew: ובאבנט בד למעוטי את המעיל כי אבנט מכפר על הרהור הלב היינו שלא יקבל האדם תקיפות מזה שמכיר את שורשו לומר שאין לו שום חלק בזה שנמצא אצלו לפעמים הרהור רע לכן כתיב אבנט בד שמכפר על הרהור הלב והוא כענין שנאמר ולא תתורו אחרי לבבכם ואחרי עיניכם היינו שאם יברר האדם את עצמו מצדו היטב אז לא יארע לו שום הרהור רע כלל.
records.targetEnglish: “With a linen sash” excludes the robe. The sash atones for thoughts of the heart: a person should not take confidence from recognizing his root and say that he has no part in the evil thought that sometimes occurs to him. Therefore Scripture specifies a linen sash, which atones for thoughts of the heart. It is like what is said, “Do not stray after your hearts and after your eyes”: if a person thoroughly clarifies himself from his own side, no evil thought will occur to him at all.
records.explanation: In its Yom Kippur account, Sod Yesharim rejects a specific form of premature assurance: knowledge of one’s holy root must not become an excuse to dismiss the work of clarifying the heart. That directly illuminates Rav Tzadok’s warning that the Chanukah illumination is a beginning, while the eye and heart still require attention. The target’s strong ideal is kept in its own words; it is not used to erase the distinction between intentional cultivation and an involuntary passing thought.

records.originHebrew: וְיָוָן נִמְשַׁל לְשָׂעִיר בְּדָנִיֵּאל דִּכְתִיב: "וְהַצָּפִיר הַשָּׂעִיר מֶלֶךְ יָוָן", וְהֵמָּה הַקְּלִפָּה שֶׁל חֹשֶׁךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה): "'וְחֹשֶׁךְ' זֶה יָוָן שֶׁהֶחְשִׁיכוּ עֵינֵיהֶם שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל". וְאִיתָא בִּמְגִלַּת תַּעֲנִית: "בִּשְׁמוֹנָה בְּטֵבֵת נִכְתְּבָה הַתּוֹרָה יְוָנִית וְהַחֹשֶׁךְ בָּא לָעוֹלָם שְׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים", וְהַיְנוּ בְּחִינַת הַחֲשֵׁכוּת שֶׁל חָכְמַת יְוָנִית, שֶׁהֵם הֶעְתִּיקוּ הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב וְאָמְרוּ "אָנוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב מִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא כִּי תִשָּׂא ל״ד), הֲגַם שֶׁעוֹבְדֵי עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וְעוֹשִׂים כָּל שֶׁחֲפֵצִים, הֵם מַלְבִּישִׁים אֶת הַתּוֹרָה לְדִבְרֵי רוּחַ.
records.originEnglish: Greece is compared to a goat in Daniel: “The shaggy goat is the king of Greece.” They are the shell of darkness, as Genesis Rabbah says: “‘Darkness’—this is Greece, which darkened Israel’s eyes.” Megillat Ta’anit states: “On the eighth of Tevet the Torah was written in Greek, and darkness came into the world for three days.” This is the darkness of Greek wisdom: they copied the Written Torah and said, “We are Israel,” as stated in Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Tissa 34. Although they worship idols and do whatever they desire, they clothe the Torah in empty words.
records.themeTitle: Torah must reach the heart rather than serve an independent desire
records.themeSummary: The paragraph condemns appropriating Torah’s words while continuing to follow idolatry and self-will. Its darkness is the separation of the text from the inward allegiance that the Torah teaches.
records.targetRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 7:1
records.targetHebrew: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הַתּוֹרָה נִכְתְּבָה בַּאֵר הֵיטֵב בְּשִׁבְעִים לָשׁוֹן [סוֹטָה ל״ב עַמּוּד א׳], כִּי מִצַּד הַכְּתָב שֶׁהוּא הִתְגַּלּוּת הַחָכְמָה נִתְגַּלָּה לְכָל בָּאֵי עוֹלָם; וְיֵשׁ חָכְמָה בָּאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם לְהַשִּׂיג גַּם כֵּן הַכָּרַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהִשִּׂיגוּ כָּל פִילוֹסוֹפֵי יָוָן וַעֲרָב הַקַּדְמוֹנִים מֵחָכְמָתָם גַּם כֵּן; רַק מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא נִשְׁתַּנָּה עַל יְדֵי זֶה לִבָּם בְּקוֹצוֹ שֶׁל יוֹ״ד, וְלֹא הָיָה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא דָּר בִּלְבָבָם כְּלָל, רַק בְּלִבּוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁלָּהֶם נִמְסַר הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, פֵּרוּשׁ: הִתְגַּלּוּת הַבִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב עַל יְדֵי הַדִּבּוּר; וּלְכָךְ: "דְּבָרִים שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה אִי אַתָּה רַשַּׁאי לְאָמְרָם בִּכְתָב" (גִּטִּין ס׳ עַמּוּד ב׳), כִּי עִקַּר דְּבָרִים שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה בַּדִּבּוּר שֶׁעַל יָדוֹ מִתְגַּלֶּה מַה שֶּׁבַּלֵּב. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל לְשׁוֹן חַכְמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּכָל מָקוֹם: "אַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי פְּלוֹנִי", כִּי כָּל הַמֵּימְרוֹת שֶׁלָּהֶם הָיָה כְּפִי לִבּוֹ, וּבִמְקוֹם "אַדַּעְתֵּיהּ" אָמְרוּ "אַלִּיבָּא", שֶׁהוּא מִן הַלֵּב.
records.targetEnglish: Nevertheless, the Torah was written “very clearly” in seventy languages, for from the aspect of writing—which reveals wisdom—it was revealed to everyone in the world. There is wisdom among the nations, enabling them also to attain recognition of God, as the ancient Greek and Arab philosophers attained through their wisdom. Yet through this their heart did not change by even the point of a yod, and the Holy One, blessed be He, did not dwell in their hearts, but only in the hearts of Israel, to whom the Oral Torah was entrusted. This means the revelation, through speech, of the understanding within the heart. Therefore, “Things that are oral you may not say in writing,” for the essence of oral teachings is speech, through which what is in the heart becomes revealed. As I heard concerning the Sages’ expression everywhere, “According to the heart of Rabbi So-and-so”: all their statements followed their heart. Instead of saying “according to his opinion,” they said “according to his heart,” because it came from the heart.
records.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim makes the distinction behind this criticism explicit. Torah can be written in many languages, and intellectual recognition can be real; the missing element in the criticized philosophy is the transformation and allegiance of the heart. The Oral Torah reveals that lived understanding through a teacher’s speech. This guards against reading Chanukah 21 as saying that another language by itself is the defect: the author’s stated issue is wisdom separated from the heart’s service.

records.originHebrew: וְגַם אָמְרוּ (פֶּרֶק א׳ מִמַּסֶּכֶת סוֹפְרִים): "כְּשֶׁהֶעְתִּיקוּ הַתּוֹרָה יְוָנִית וְהָיָה הַיּוֹם קָשֶׁה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל כַּיּוֹם שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה הָעֵגֶל"; וְהַיְנוּ כִּי בְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה הָיָה נִשְׁפַּע הֶאָרָה גְּדוֹלָה, וְאַחַר כָּךְ כְּשֶׁעָשׂוּ הָעֵגֶל וְנִשְׁבְּרוּ הַלֻּחוֹת חָזַר הַחֲשֵׁכוּת; וּכְעִנְיַן הַזֶּה הָיָה בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁעָמְדָה יָוָן "לְהַשְׁכִּיחָם תּוֹרָתֶךָ וּלְהַעֲבִירָם מֵחֻקֵּי רְצוֹנָךְ", וְזֶה הָיָה בְּחֹדֶשׁ טֵבֵת שֶׁמַּזָּלוֹ גְּדִי שֶׁהוּא בְּחִינַת הַחֲשֵׁכוּת. וְדַוְקָא אָז פָּעֲלוּ בְּנֵס עַל יְדֵי מְסִירַת נַפְשָׁם לְהָאִיר מִתּוֹךְ הַחֹשֶׁךְ בְּיֶתֶר שְׂאֵת, עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב׳ קפ״ד עַמּוּד א׳): "דְּלֵית נְהוֹרָא אֶלָּא הַהוּא דְּנָפֵיק מִגּוֹ חֲשׁוֹכָא", וְהַיְנוּ כִּבְרִיָּתוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם; וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (שַׁבָּת ק״ל עַמּוּד א׳): "כָּל מִצְוָה שֶׁמָּסְרוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל עַצְמָם עֲלֵיהֶם לְמִיתָה וְכוּלֵיהּ עֲדַיִן הִיא מֻחְזֶקֶת בְּיָדָם", וְהַיְנוּ שֶׁפָּעֲלוּ עַל יְדֵי זֶה דַּוְקָא לִהְיוֹת נֶחְקָק הַחֻקֵּי חַיִּים בַּלֵּב. וְזֶה גַּם כֵּן הָרֶמֶז "וְאֵת עֹרֹת גְּדָיֵי הָעִזִּים הִלְבִּישָׁה עַל יָדָיו", כִּי יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם קִבֵּל הַבְּרָכוֹת דַּוְקָא עַל יְדֵי הַלְּבוּשׁ שֶׁל גְּדָיֵי הָעִזִּים שֶׁהוּא בְּחִינַת הַשָּׂעִיר, דְּ"לֵית נְהוֹרָא אֶלָּא הַהוּא דְּנָפֵיק מִגּוֹ חֲשׁוֹכָא".
records.originEnglish: They also said in the first chapter of Massekhet Soferim: “When they copied the Torah into Greek, the day was as hard for Israel as the day the calf was made.” At the giving of the Torah a great illumination was bestowed; afterward, when they made the calf and the tablets were broken, darkness returned. Something of this kind occurred when Greece arose “to make them forget Your Torah and to turn them away from the statutes of Your will.” This was in Tevet, whose sign is the kid, the quality of darkness. Precisely then, through their readiness to give their lives, they brought about the miracle of shining out of darkness with greater strength, in the manner of the Zohar’s saying, “There is no light except that which emerges from darkness.” This follows the creation of the world. As Shabbat 130a says, “Every commandment for which Israel gave themselves over to death … is still firmly held by them”: through precisely this they caused the statutes of life to be engraved within the heart. This is also the hint in “She clothed his hands with the skins of the goat kids.” Jacob our father received the blessings precisely through the garment of goat skins, the quality of the goat, for “there is no light except that which emerges from darkness.”
records.themeTitle: Fidelity within darkness engraves the commandment in the heart
records.themeSummary: The original illumination can be lost from view. Rav Tzadok explains how fidelity under opposition can produce a deeper, lasting inscription of the commandments, using both Chanukah and Jacob’s goat-skin garment.
records.targetHebrew: בהבדלה בתפלה הנוסח ותלמדנו לעשות חוקי רצונך וכמו"כ אומרים בנוסח עה"נ להשכיחם תורתך ולהעבירם מחקי רצונך. ונראה שמרמז בזה כעין שרומז בכהאריז"ל בר"ת חש"מ מתיבת חשמונאי שהוא ר"ת חודש שבת מילה שרצו לבטל מישראל וג' מצות אלו נקראים חוקי רצונך מפני שהם נחקקים לאות דייקא בנפשות ישראל שבזה הם נבדלים מן העכו"ם. ולטעם זה עמדו היונים לבטל מישראל דייקא שלש מצות האלו. מפני שבהם דייקא נחקק קדושת ישראל. כי קדושת שבת כתיב בני ובין בנ"י אות היא לעולם. וקדושת המילה הוא ג"כ רק אות לישראל כידוע וכמ"ש (נדרים לא:) שאני נהנה למולים אסור בערלי ישראל וכו'. וקדושת החודש הוא רק לישראל כש"נ החודש הזה לכם הגם שחשבון המולד ידוע לכל אמנם הכח הזה ניתן דייקא לישראל שיוכלו לקדש החודש אפילו קודם המולד או לאחריו. וכמ"ש (ר"ה כה.) אתם אפי' שוגגין אתם אפי' מזידין כו'.
records.targetEnglish: In the havdalah within prayer the wording is, “You taught us to perform the statutes of Your will”; similarly, in Al HaNissim we say, “to make them forget Your Torah and turn them away from the statutes of Your will.” It seems that this hints at what the Ari’s writings suggest through the letters chet, shin, mem in Chashmonai: chodesh, Shabbat, milah—month, Sabbath, circumcision—which they wished to abolish from Israel. These three commandments are called “the statutes of Your will” because they are engraved specifically as a sign within the souls of Israel, through which they are distinguished from the nations. For this reason the Greeks arose to abolish specifically these three commandments from Israel, since Israel’s holiness is engraved precisely through them. Concerning the holiness of Shabbat it is written, “Between Me and the children of Israel it is a sign forever.” The holiness of circumcision likewise is a sign specifically for Israel, as is known; as Nedarim 31b states, “One who vows, ‘I may not benefit from the circumcised,’ is forbidden to benefit from uncircumcised Israelites ….” The holiness of the month also belongs specifically to Israel, as it says, “This month is for you.” Although the calculation of the new moon is known to everyone, this power was given specifically to Israel: they can sanctify the month even before the conjunction or after it. As Rosh Hashanah 25a says, “‘You’—even when mistaken; ‘you’—even when deliberate ….”
records.explanation: Miketz identifies the “statutes” that Rav Tzadok says became engraved in the heart: the sanctification of the month, Shabbat, and circumcision, each constituting an embodied or lived sign of the covenant. It explains why suppressing these commandments attacks more than abstract knowledge. Chanukah 21 supplies the further historical-spiritual step: steadfastness under that suppression establishes the inscription more deeply.

records.originHebrew: וְגַם אָמְרוּ (פֶּרֶק א׳ מִמַּסֶּכֶת סוֹפְרִים): "כְּשֶׁהֶעְתִּיקוּ הַתּוֹרָה יְוָנִית וְהָיָה הַיּוֹם קָשֶׁה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל כַּיּוֹם שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה הָעֵגֶל"; וְהַיְנוּ כִּי בְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה הָיָה נִשְׁפַּע הֶאָרָה גְּדוֹלָה, וְאַחַר כָּךְ כְּשֶׁעָשׂוּ הָעֵגֶל וְנִשְׁבְּרוּ הַלֻּחוֹת חָזַר הַחֲשֵׁכוּת; וּכְעִנְיַן הַזֶּה הָיָה בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁעָמְדָה יָוָן "לְהַשְׁכִּיחָם תּוֹרָתֶךָ וּלְהַעֲבִירָם מֵחֻקֵּי רְצוֹנָךְ", וְזֶה הָיָה בְּחֹדֶשׁ טֵבֵת שֶׁמַּזָּלוֹ גְּדִי שֶׁהוּא בְּחִינַת הַחֲשֵׁכוּת. וְדַוְקָא אָז פָּעֲלוּ בְּנֵס עַל יְדֵי מְסִירַת נַפְשָׁם לְהָאִיר מִתּוֹךְ הַחֹשֶׁךְ בְּיֶתֶר שְׂאֵת, עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב׳ קפ״ד עַמּוּד א׳): "דְּלֵית נְהוֹרָא אֶלָּא הַהוּא דְּנָפֵיק מִגּוֹ חֲשׁוֹכָא", וְהַיְנוּ כִּבְרִיָּתוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם; וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (שַׁבָּת ק״ל עַמּוּד א׳): "כָּל מִצְוָה שֶׁמָּסְרוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל עַצְמָם עֲלֵיהֶם לְמִיתָה וְכוּלֵיהּ עֲדַיִן הִיא מֻחְזֶקֶת בְּיָדָם", וְהַיְנוּ שֶׁפָּעֲלוּ עַל יְדֵי זֶה דַּוְקָא לִהְיוֹת נֶחְקָק הַחֻקֵּי חַיִּים בַּלֵּב. וְזֶה גַּם כֵּן הָרֶמֶז "וְאֵת עֹרֹת גְּדָיֵי הָעִזִּים הִלְבִּישָׁה עַל יָדָיו", כִּי יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם קִבֵּל הַבְּרָכוֹת דַּוְקָא עַל יְדֵי הַלְּבוּשׁ שֶׁל גְּדָיֵי הָעִזִּים שֶׁהוּא בְּחִינַת הַשָּׂעִיר, דְּ"לֵית נְהוֹרָא אֶלָּא הַהוּא דְּנָפֵיק מִגּוֹ חֲשׁוֹכָא".
records.originEnglish: They also said in the first chapter of Massekhet Soferim: “When they copied the Torah into Greek, the day was as hard for Israel as the day the calf was made.” At the giving of the Torah a great illumination was bestowed; afterward, when they made the calf and the tablets were broken, darkness returned. Something of this kind occurred when Greece arose “to make them forget Your Torah and to turn them away from the statutes of Your will.” This was in Tevet, whose sign is the kid, the quality of darkness. Precisely then, through their readiness to give their lives, they brought about the miracle of shining out of darkness with greater strength, in the manner of the Zohar’s saying, “There is no light except that which emerges from darkness.” This follows the creation of the world. As Shabbat 130a says, “Every commandment for which Israel gave themselves over to death … is still firmly held by them”: through precisely this they caused the statutes of life to be engraved within the heart. This is also the hint in “She clothed his hands with the skins of the goat kids.” Jacob our father received the blessings precisely through the garment of goat skins, the quality of the goat, for “there is no light except that which emerges from darkness.”

records.targetHebrew: היינו שישראל הי' צריכין לברר שיהי' רואים מפורש החילוק וההבדל מהצאן של ישראל שהוא צאן של מצוה להצאן של מצרים שהוא צאן של ע"ז כי צאן רומז על הערב שהוא קודם לבוקר כענין שמצינו בגמ' (שבת ע"ז:) מ"ט עיזי מסגן ברישא והדר אימרי כברייתו של עולם ברישא חשוכא והדר נהורא דכתיב ויהי ערב ויהי בוקר וביאר אאמו"ר הגה"ק זללה"ה שעל זה הענין רמזו ז"ל שע"ז של מצרים הי' צאן היינו שכל עבודתם הי' להחושך הקודם לאור והי' עושים אותו החושך קדמאה לדחלא דלהון שיהי' כל מעשיהם במחשוך ולקבל כל ההשפעות בלי שום עבודה רק למעלה מדעתם וזה נקרא חושך שהולכים בלי דעת כן אור נקרא מה שהולך האדם בדעת ובחשבון ועל זה הענין איתא שם אתקשר צאן בצאן היינו כי לפי הנראה נמשכין ישראל ג"כ בלי דעת וחשבון למעלה מתפיסת דעתם עד שנקראו עמא פזוזא דקדמיתו פימייכו לאודנייכו וכו' שאינם מחשבין כלל בדעתם אם יהי' בכוחם לסבול או לאו ועל זה איתא שם בדא אתקשרו ישראל ארבע מאה שנין וכו' היינו עד שיתברר מפורש החילוק וההבדל לאתפרשא מקטרוי היינו שיהי' ניכר מפורש אשר כל המכוון של ישראל בזה שנמשכים למעלה מתפיסת דעתם הוא רק למען שיגיעו ע"י זה להמקור משורש רצונו ית' שהוא אור הבהיר היותר נעלה מזה האור שנקרא מצד אדם אור והמשכה כזו בלי דעת וחשבון נקרא צאן של מצוה משא"כ הצאן של מצרים נקרא ע"ז כי הם אינם רוצים להסתכל באור כי אומרים שהרצון ית' האציל במכוון ערב קודם לבוקר למען להסתיר מעיני אדם את האור כדי שילך תמיד בחושך ולא באור ושיהי' במחשוך מעשיו ועל אותו הבירור איתא שם ולא יכול לאתפרשא מקטרוי וכו' שבאמת הוא הבדל דק מאוד ואינו בניקל כ"כ להראות מפורש לעיני אדם זה החילוק מצאן לצאן:
records.targetEnglish: Israel had to clarify the difference so that it could be seen explicitly: between Israel’s flock, a flock for a commandment, and Egypt’s flock, a flock of idolatry. A flock hints at the evening before the morning, as the Gemara asks: “Why do goats walk first and then sheep? Like the world’s creation: first darkness and then light, as it says, ‘There was evening and there was morning.’” My holy father explained that this is what the Sages meant in saying that Egypt’s idolatry was the flock. All their service was directed to the darkness preceding the light; they made that primordial darkness their object of fear, so that all their deeds would remain in darkness and they could receive every flow of good without any service, above their understanding. This is called darkness: proceeding without knowledge. Light is when a person proceeds with knowledge and reckoning. The Zohar says concerning this, “Flock was bound to flock”: outwardly, Israel too follow without knowledge or calculation, above their apprehension. They were even called “a hasty people, who put your mouth before your ears,” not calculating whether they would have the strength to bear it. Of this it says that Israel were bound in this for four hundred years, until the distinction would be explicitly clarified and separated from its knot. It would become apparent that Israel’s entire purpose in following beyond their apprehension was to reach the source at the root of His will, which is a light far higher than the light called light from the human side. Such following without knowledge and reckoning is called a flock of a commandment. Egypt’s flock, by contrast, is called idolatry: they do not wish to look at the light. They say that His will intentionally emanated evening before morning in order to conceal the light from human eyes, so that a person would always walk in darkness and not in light, with deeds in darkness. The Zohar speaks of the clarification’s not being easily untied because this is truly a very fine distinction; it is not easy to show the difference between flock and flock explicitly to human eyes.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains a crucial distinction within the same goats-before-sheep image. Going beyond present understanding can be faithful movement toward the divine source, or a wish to keep one’s deeds permanently outside the light. This illuminates why the darkness of Jacob’s garment and Chanukah can become an opening to greater light: the direction of the person’s fidelity matters. The source expressly calls that distinction subtle, rather than making every plunge into darkness a holy act.
