records.originHebrew: וְהֲגַם שֶׁבְּנֵס פּוּרִים מְבָרְכִין גַּם כֵּן עַל נִסִּים שֶׁהָיָה בַּזְּמַן הֶעָבָר, הוּא גַּם כֵּן מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהָיָה עוֹד בִּימֵי הַנְּבִיאִים, וְיָדְעוּ שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא הִסְכִּים לָזֶה, וּכְמַה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "קִיְּמוּ וְקִבְּלוּ" קִיְּמוּ לְמַעְלָה מַה שֶּׁקִּבְּלוּ לְמַטָּה, וּמִזֶּה לָמְדוּ שֶׁאֶסְתֵּר בְּרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ נֶאֶמְרָה ( כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב מְגִלָּה ז׳ עַמּוּד א׳ ), וְהוּא עוֹד בְּחִינַת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב; מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בַּחֲנֻכָּה שֶׁהָיָה לְאַחַר שֶׁפָּסְקָה הַנְּבוּאָה, רַק מִצַּד מִצְוַת חֲכָמִים לְבַד. וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר בָּזֶה, שֶׁדַּוְקָא בְּנֵס זֶה שֶׁל חֲנֻכָּה רָאוּ חֲכָמִים שֶׁמּוֹפִיעַ קְדֻשַּׁת הַנֵּס עַל הַזְּמַן, וְלָכֵן קָבְעוּ הַמִּצְוָה וְהַבְּרָכָה עַל הַזְּמַן.
records.originEnglish: Although on Purim too we bless for miracles that occurred in the past, this is also because it was still in the days of the prophets, and they knew that the Holy One, blessed be He, had agreed to it. As it says, “They confirmed and accepted”: they confirmed above what had been accepted below. From this they learned that Esther was spoken through the holy spirit, as stated in Megillah 7a, and it still belongs to the aspect of Written Torah. Chanukah, however, occurred after prophecy had ceased and rests solely on the Sages’ commandment. We may say that, specifically in this miracle of Chanukah, the Sages saw that the miracle’s holiness shines upon the time; they therefore established the commandment and the blessing in relation to the time.
records.themeTitle: The enduring deliverance that makes the date holy
records.themeSummary: After distinguishing a past rescue from a holiness that returns each year, Rav Tzadok asks how the Sages could institute Chanukah once prophecy had ceased.
records.targetHebrew: אֲבָל הַנֵּס דַּחֲנֻכָּה, שֶׁהָיָה הַצָּלָה מִשְּׁמָד לְבַד, לֹא נִקְבְּעוּ אֶלָּא לְהַלֵּל וּלְהוֹדוֹת וְלֹא שׁוּם עוֹנֶג גּוּפָנִי, כִּי לֹא הָיְתָה הַצָּלַת גּוּפוֹת. וְהַמִּצְוָה שֶׁבּוֹ בְּהַדְלָקַת הַנֵּר, כִּי זֶהוּ עִיקַּר הַיְשׁוּעָה, בְּ"אוֹרָה — זוֹ תּוֹרָה", וְעַל כֵּן לֹא נִיתְּנָה לִכְתֹּב, כִּי אֵין בּוֹ הִתְלַבְּשׁוּת בִּלְבוּשׁ גּוּפָנִי בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וְהוּא כְּכָל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שֶׁ"אִי אַתָּה רַשַּׁאי לְאָמְרָם בִּכְתָב". שֶׁיְשׁוּעָה זוֹ שֶׁנִּשְׁאֲרָה קָבוּעַ וְקַיָּים לְדוֹרוֹת כְּכָל קְדֻשַּׁת הַזְּמַנִּים שֶׁנִּשְׁאָר בְּאוֹתוֹ זְמַן לְעוֹלָם, קְדֻשָּׁה זוֹ אֵינָהּ אֶלָּא יְשׁוּעַת הַנֶּפֶשׁ וְהַשֵּׂכֶל שֶׁלֹּא יִטַּמָּא בְּחָכְמַת בְּנֵי נֵכָר, שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד חָכְמַת חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה
records.targetEnglish: But the miracle of Chanukah was deliverance from forced abandonment of the faith alone. Its days were established only for praise and thanksgiving, without any bodily pleasure, because it was not a deliverance of bodies. Its commandment is the lighting of the lamp, for this is the essential deliverance: “Light” is Torah. It was therefore not given to be written, because it has no embodiment in a bodily garment in this world. It is like all Oral Torah, of which “you are not permitted to put these matters in writing.” This deliverance remained fixed and enduring for generations, like every holiness of the appointed times that remains in that time forever. This holiness is solely the deliverance of the soul and intellect, so that they will not be defiled by the wisdom of foreigners, which opposes the wisdom of Israel’s Sages in Oral Torah.
records.explanation: Resisei identifies what endures after the historical rescue: the soul’s and intellect’s freedom to receive Oral Torah. It expressly connects that enduring deliverance with the holiness that remains in the same time forever, and connects Chanukah’s unwritten character with Oral Torah. This supplies the content of the returning holiness that the origin says the Sages perceived; the explanation concerns the religious character of the commemoration, not a claim that no physical danger accompanied the war.

records.originHebrew: וְעַל זֶה מְסַיֵּם: שֶׁאֵין רַשָּׁאִים לוֹמַר כֵּן אַף עַל מִצְוָה זוֹ שֶׁהוּא מוֹרֶה עַל הוֹפָעַת קְדֻשָּׁה בַּזְּמַן, לָמָּה? שֶׁאַף עַל דִּבְרֵיהֶם אֲנִי מַסְכִּים, גַּם מַה שֶּׁגּוֹזְרִים עַל הַשְׁרָאַת קְדֻשַּׁת הַנֵּס בַּזְּמַן, כְּמַה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְתִגְזַר אֹמֶר וְיָקָם לָךְ", וְהַיְנוּ אַף אֲמִירָה בְּעָלְמָא.
records.originEnglish: The Midrash concludes that one may not refuse to fulfill the elders’ commandment even in this case, where the commandment signifies the manifestation of holiness in time. Why? Because God says, “I agree also to their words”—including what they decree concerning the indwelling of the miracle’s holiness in time. As it says, “You shall decree a word, and it shall be established for you”; that is, even a mere utterance.

records.targetHebrew: וְגַם יֵשׁ לוֹמַר שֶׁהָיָה עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וְתִגְזַר אֹמֶר וְיָקָם לָךְ״ (אִיּוֹב כ״ב:כ״ח), ״צַדִּיק גּוֹזֵר וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְקַיֵּים״ כִּי נַעֲשָׂה הוּא מַכְרִיעַ בְּבֵית דִּין שֶׁל מַעְלָה, וַהֲלָכָה כְּמוֹתוֹ בִּגְזֵירוֹתָיו נֶגֶד גְּזֵירַת דִּינָא עִילָּאָה כִּי כָּל הַמִּשְׁפָּטִים בְּכָל עוֹלָמוֹת עֶלְיוֹנִים הַכֹּל הוּא עַל פִּי הַתּוֹרָה, וְהַתּוֹרָה כְּבָר נִמְסְרָה לַתַּחְתּוֹנִים וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ לְעִנְיַן קְבִיעַת רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה: ״אֲנִי וְאַתֶּם נֵלֵךְ לְבֵית דִּין שֶׁל מַטָּה, וְאִם עִיבְּרוּ בֵּית דִּין הַחֹדֶשׁ, הַדִּינִין שֶׁל מַעְלָה מִתְבַּטְּלִין מֵאוֹתוֹ יוֹם״ וְכֵן בְּכָל סְפֵיקוֹת שֶׁבְּעִנְיְנֵי הַתּוֹרָה, כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁמַּכְרִיעִים חֲכָמִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כֵּן הוּא הַהַכְרָעָה בְּכָל עוֹלָמוֹת עֶלְיוֹנִים
records.targetEnglish: We may also say that this intervention on Aher’s behalf occurred in the manner of the verse, “You shall decree a word, and it shall be established for you” (Job 22:28): “A righteous person decrees and the Holy One, blessed be He, fulfills.” For the righteous person becomes the deciding authority in the heavenly court, and the ruling follows his decrees against the decree of heavenly judgment. All judgments in all the upper worlds are according to Torah, and Torah has already been handed over to those below. As they said concerning the appointment of Rosh Hashanah: “I and you will go to the earthly court”; and if the court extends the month, the heavenly judgments are canceled for that day. So too, in every uncertainty concerning Torah, the decision made by the Sages in this world is the decision in all the upper worlds.
records.explanation: Takanat explains the mechanism behind the same verse: heaven judges according to Torah, and authority to decide Torah has been entrusted to the earthly Sages. Its concrete example is especially exact here—the earthly court’s calendar decision changes the day of heavenly judgment. The larger passage concerns Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yohanan’s ruling about Aher’s repentance; the calendar example provides an analogy for the origin’s extension of divine agreement to Chanukah’s sanctified time, without identifying the two enactments as the same law.

records.targetHebrew: הרי שכל הנהגת העולם מסר השי"ת ביד ישראל לכך נאמר קודם כל המועדים פ' שבת להורות שכמה יש לו להאדם כח באשר תקראו אתם רק כפי שמכיר בקדושת שבת הקבוע וקיימא מצדו ית' כן מוסר לו השי"ת כח לקדש את הזמנים אשר תקראו אתם
records.targetEnglish: Thus God entrusted all the world’s governance to Israel. Therefore, the passage about Shabbat is stated before all the festivals, to teach that the extent of a person’s power in “which you shall proclaim” corresponds to the extent that the person recognizes the holiness of Shabbat, fixed and enduring from God’s side. In that measure God entrusts the person with power to sanctify the appointed times: “which you shall proclaim.”
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim supplies the condition within the power to sanctify time: Israel’s authority is received through recognizing holiness that already comes from God. Its full paragraph contrasts Shabbat’s fixed holiness with the festivals determined by Israel and concludes that this divine accommodation is freely willed, not forced upon God. This illuminates the origin’s language of God agreeing to the elders’ words: their effective action belongs within His grant of authority.

records.targetHebrew: ואחר זה נאמר בקרבנות חנוכת הנשיאים שזה מרמז על עצם כח התחדשות של תורה שבעל פה מה שהאדם מחדש מלבו שכל נשיא המציא לעצמו מלבו להביא מספר הקרבנות הללו כדאיתא במדרש (במדרש רבה פ' י"ב) על הפ' ויביאו את קרבנם שכולם הביאו מעצמם את כל קרבנם ביום הראשון וע"פ הדיבור הקריב אחר כך כל אחד ביומו המיוחד לו. והנה פרט בכל נשיא ונשיא מספר הקרבנות ומנחתם ומשקל הכלים אם שכולם הקריבו בשוה שנראה כמיותר שהיה יכול לכתוב וכן ביום השני הקריב נשיא פ' כמספר הראשון וכן בכולם. מזה מוכיח המ"ר שכל אחד היה לו כוונות אחרות בהקרבתו לזה פרט בכל אחד במיוחד. מזה נוכל להבין כח התחדשות של תורה שבעל פה אף על פי ששני ב"א עושים מעשה בתבנית אחד עכ"ז יש לכל אחד ענין ומדרגה בפ"ע לפי ערך הכנת לבו בפנימיות הענין והעיקר אחר כונת הלב הדברים אמורים
records.targetEnglish: After this comes the account of the princes’ dedication offerings. This alludes to the essential power of renewal in Oral Torah: what a person originates from the heart. Each prince himself conceived in his heart the bringing of these quantities of offerings. As Midrash Rabbah, chapter 12, explains on “They brought their offering,” they all brought their entire offering on their own initiative on the first day; afterwards, by the divine word, each offered on his own appointed day. Scripture details for each individual prince the number of offerings and their meal offerings, and the weight of the vessels, although all offered equally. This appears superfluous, for it could have written that on the second day a particular prince offered the same number as the first, and similarly for all of them. From this Midrash Rabbah demonstrates that each had different intentions in his offering, and therefore Scripture details each separately. From this we can understand the power of renewal in Oral Torah: even if two people perform an act of identical form, each nevertheless has a distinct meaning and level according to the preparation of the heart in the inner matter. The essential consideration is the intention of the heart.
records.explanation: Nasso explains what the princes contributed through their own initiative: each brought an inward intention that was not exhausted by the identical outward quantities. God then assigned each offering its day. Rav Tzadok explicitly treats this as the power of innovation in Oral Torah. It gives specific content to the origin’s claim that the princes’ dedication demonstrates divine agreement with human wisdom, and connects that dedication to the Sages’ later creative authority.

records.targetHebrew: איתא במדרש (תנחומא פקודי י"א) והובא (ברש"י ז"ל על מקומו) שלא היה יכולין להקימו וכו' אמר משה לפני הקב"ה איני יודע להעמידו. א"ל הקב"ה עסוק אתה בידך נראה כמקימו והוא נזקף וקם מאליו, וזה שנאמר הוקם המשכן הוקם מאליו. הענין בזה כמו שביאר כבוד אאמו"ר זללה"ה, שאחר כל העבודות והבירורים שאדם מברר את עצמו, לא שייך לומר שבירר את עצמו עד הגמר, כי מי יאמר זכיתי לבי. ורק כן הציב השי"ת שאדם יעבוד את השי"ת בכל כחו עד מקום שידו מגעת, ואז כשהאדם עובד בכל כחו, אז חותם השי"ת על כל עבודתו ונקראת על שם האדם
records.targetEnglish: The Midrash (Tanchuma, Pekudei 11), cited by Rashi at the verse, says that they could not erect it, and so forth. Moses said before the Holy One, blessed be He: “I do not know how to set it up.” The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: “Engage with it using your hands; you will appear to be erecting it, and it will straighten and stand by itself.” This is what is meant by “the Mishkan was erected”: it was erected by itself. The meaning, as my revered father and teacher, of blessed memory, explained, is that after all the service and refinement through which a person refines himself, it is inappropriate to say that he has refined himself to completion, for “Who can say, ‘I have purified my heart’?” God has simply established that a person should serve Him with all his strength, as far as his hand can reach. When the person serves with all his strength, God then sets His seal upon all that service, and it is attributed to the person.
records.explanation: Tiferet explains how a sanctuary can arise through human hands while its completion still comes from God. Moses must work, yet the Mishkan stands through divine confirmation; the completed work is then credited to the person. This gives a precise account of the origin’s “indwelling of holiness through the work of the wise builders’ hands.” The rest of the target paragraph applies this to Israel’s purified intention and Moses’ blessing that the Divine Presence dwell in their handiwork.
